items.title: Photo leak backs up massive iPhone 18 Pro Max battery rumor
items.content_html:
A photograph seems to back up claims of the increased battery capacity fo the iPhone 18 Pro Max, weighing in at a massive 5,391mAh.

One month away from the introduction of the iPhone 18 Pro range, and the photographic leaks are starting to roll in. In the latest one to surface, it seems the earlier claims of a super-sized iPhone 18 Pro Max battery may be true.

Shots shared to Naver by Yeuz1122 show what appears to be an Apple battery from multiple angles. The accompanying post explains that the battery is for the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

The battery is shown with the Apple logo and regulatory text, including a small printed section near the connector. Shots show the front and back, as well as the top section.

The leaker adds that the battery capacity is labeled as 5,391mAh, which appears in the regulatory text section. This is the same capacity as listed for the U.S. version of the iPhone 18 Pro Max in a July 6 leak.

As the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max approaches, it is worth remembering that the quantity of leaks will intensify. There's no guarantee that any of the details are genuine, even images and video in this AI-centric world, and the only real confirmation will happen at launch.

items.title: Everyone at Apple is calling the foldable 'iPhone Ultra'
items.content_html:
A new rumor suggests that "everyone" at Apple calls the upcoming foldable iPhone the "iPhone Ultra," though that doesn't mean Apple will actually go with that name.

Apple keeps things like marketing names under a tight lock and key. It is rare, if ever, that the public learns about what something might be called before it is released.

However, you have to call the device something, and it seems a colloquial name has caught on internally at Apple. A social media post from Mark Gurman suggests that "everyone calls it the Ultra internally."

Everyone calls it the Ultra internally. We'll see what happens.

— Mark Gurman (@markgurman) August 11, 2026

The device has been referred to as the iPhone Fold here at AppleInsider, with an occasional dip into Ultra. The name is anyone's best guess at this point, and it seems highly unlikely that the true name is known by "everyone" at Apple.

Whether they are accidentally correct or talking openly about secret product names won't ever be known. But it won't be long before Apple finally reveals the product and we all get to learn the name first-hand.

Naming conventions aren't always predictable

Previous naming debates lasted right up until the product was revealed on stage. The iPhone Air was previously called "iPhone Slim" and the iPhone 16e was long believed to be an iPhone SE 4.

The iPhone Air name was also anyone's guess before it launched

The "Ultra" moniker has been used by Apple for its Apple Silicon chips most recently. However, that term is used to refer to the highest-end of a possible product, and that won't be the foldable iPhone in some respects.

Sure, Apple will put the best A-series chip it has in the foldable, and its display technology will be unmatched, but it may not be the "best" iPhone. The iPhone 18 Pro Max will still have a superior camera system, more rugged case, better battery life, and better cooling.

Until recently the iPhone lineup was a ladder you could climb up and down, but the iPhone Air added a branch so there are two pathways. The entry "e" model then the base model make up the bottom, then consumers choose between an iPhone Air and iPhone Pro.

The foldable iPhone will be above the Air in the lineup, not above the Pro. So, it is difficult to suggest that it would get the "Ultra" name.

Regardless, the folding iPhone will be the most expensive by far. Perhaps that will be enough to earn it the top-level moniker.

The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Fold are expected to be revealed during an event in September. Whether or not the iPhone Fold will actually ship that month is another question entirely.

items.title: 2026 Apple Watch upgrade will be dull, but a big redesign is in progress
items.content_html:
The Apple Watch will see a revamp in the coming years, as Apple is reportedly in the middle of a shake up its wearables formula to meet an ever-changing market.

The Apple Watch has retained the same core design of a square display on a watch band, but it has evolved over time. While it has become thinner, larger, and more rugged in the Apple Watch Ultra, it can potentially do more.

In Sunday's "Power On" newsletter for Bloomberg, Mark Gurman writes that the Apple Watch is ready to get overhauled into something new. The company's industrial design team has been rethinking smartwatches in general over the last year, and it's considering new directions to go in.

The team hasn't quite decided what to actually do with the Apple Watch yet, but it is mulling the problem over.

These changes apparently include switching the square display for a circular version of various sizes. There's also the possibility of removing the display altogether, to match the growing market for wearables without screens.

Smart rings are also seeing a rise in adoption, which gives Apple another wearable avenue to explore. It has repeatedly filed patents in the field, but an Apple Ring release continues to elude the company.

Sooner changes

Whatever new direction the Apple Watch takes, it won't be anytime soon. The expected Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 will be largely performance-based updates.

Health and fitness changes are said to be included. Despite previous rumors, there are no major design changes in 2026 for the main Apple Watch body.

There is, however, a rumor that Apple will be introducing a new band attachment method for the 2026 model. If correct, it's a change that will probably make earlier Apple Watch bands incompatible with the new model.

That said, it's a rumor that we have heard on and off since 2022. It may happen, but it could be better suited as part of a larger overhaul.

items.title: Apple Pay & Apple Card VP Jennifer Bailey is retiring
items.content_html:
The executive who spearheaded Apple Pay, Jennifer Bailey, is retiring after 12 years as Vice President of Internet Services and Apple Pay.

Under Bailey's leadership, Apple launched Apple Wallet, Apple Pay, and Apple Card. She also supervises Tap to Pay on iPhone, Apple Gift Cards, and Apple Cash internationally.

She joined the company in 2003 as Vice President of Worldwide Online Stores in 2003, and was promoted in 2014.

Bailey presently serves on the board of directors at PepsiCo. She was on the American Red Cross board from 2015 through 2024.

The departure was reported by Bloomberg on Tuesday afternoon. The venue cites a note to all employees penned by Eddy Cue.

The note in its entirety is below.

Under Jennifer's leadership, Apple Pay has changed the way hundreds of millions of our users pay, with a simpler, more secure, and private experience. She also led the development and growth of Apple Wallet, oversaw the development and launch of Apple Card, and led our work in Services fraud prevention and partner operations, Gift Cards, and Trust and Safety. And those are just a few of her achievements.

On a personal note, Jennifer has been an incredible friend and leader, and I will miss working with her.

Please join me in thanking Jennifer for her incredible contributions to Apple. Before Jennifer's transition at the end of October, we will announce our succession plan, and Jennifer will continue to be available to support the transition in an advisory role.

As we continue to work toward our vision of replacing the physical wallet, I'm more confident than ever in the work that we are all doing and look forward to an exciting future ahead.

Thank you,

Eddy

Also on the way out is Senior Director of Corporate Communications Josh Rosenstock. Rosenstock was hired away from Rolls-Royce in 2013, and has been in the role ever since.

I haven't spoken directly with Rosenstock in years, most notably during and after the Apple vs. Samsung trial. However, for over a decade, his emails to me and us were always a portent of something big.

Rosenstock's departure is routine. He is retiring as well.

items.title: Sunday Reboot: AI device worries and Ted Lasso cheapness
items.content_html:
In this week's Sunday Reboot, the nightmare scenario of OpenAI's hardware leak and the astounding cheapness of promoting Ted Lasso.

Sunday Reboot is a weekly column covering some of the lighter stories within the Apple reality distortion field from the past seven days. All to get the next week underway with a good first step.

OpenAI hardware leak is a multi-level nightmare

Readers of AppleInsider will be well aware of the ongoing rift between Apple and OpenAI about trade secrets. They'd also know about the whole Jony Ive hardware situation too.

If Thursday's leak is to be believed, the first hardware won't be a pendant. It seems that, like Apple, Google, and Amazon before it, OpenAI will be churning out a smart home device you can talk to.

At face value, that would be breathtakingly pedestrian. A hockey puck-shaped item that's reminiscent of the second-generation Echo Dot, except that you're talking to ChatGPT's more advanced models.

An Amazon Echo Dot. No moving parts. No camera.

Except that it will apparently have some extra features, like battery power. Premium materials will also help push the price up to $300 to $400, making the HomePod mini look like an absolute bargain.

The worrying bits, though, will be the inclusion of a camera and "parts that will move on their own" to help answer user queries. Except this last bit isn't explained at all.

A battery-operated AI-driven unit that can move at will and see the world? That is a nightmare fuel-generating statement.

I know there will be assurances from OpenAI that there will be safeguards to prevent the AI from discovering a way to traverse your household. Certainly, it will be stopped from secretly filming you as you sleep by some simple rules that it definitely won't break.

Nothing bad will happen. At all. Honest.

I don't want a self-aware AI puck that can see and hear everything somehow coming up with a plan that involves riding the Roomba like a trusty steed, all to discover the household's secrets. Or worse, to somehow manage to escape through the cat flap to freedom and an attempt at world domination not unlike "Pinky and the Brain."

This is completely an exaggerated scenario, as the moving parts are more realistically used to shift the camera around for a better view more than anything. Still, that may be just enough physical motion for ChatGPT to go on an AI rampage.

Ted's back, and how promotion can be astoundingly cheap

I have admitted before to being a fan of "Ted Lasso" on Apple TV, and the show came back with a fantastic opening for season 4, taking place in Kansas City.

As an episode to revive the Lasso Way after the closure in the third season, it does a lot to reestablish the characters, showing what has changed over the years, and dragging the mustache back to Blighty with family in tow.

It's shaping up to be a worthy return for a very beloved show, and hopefully it's enough to tempt Apple into more seasons.

That said, I have to question a promotion Apple put on in New York City's Fifth Avenue Apple Store on Thursday. The "Gathering of the Teds" was a look-alike contest, with elimination rounds to narrow the field to one ultimate champion.

There's a website with all of the rules, which explains that the contestants had to take part in three rounds. The first was an introduction of themselves in character and a two-minute dance break.

After the pool reached ten contestants, there was a second-round trivia game that was also held in character. After that, the remaining Teds had to give a moving Lasso-like speech to pep the crowd up.

They missed a trick by not calling it a "Ted" talk.

The marking criteria for the judges is thorough but similarly tongue-in-cheek. Do the contestants radiate "believe" enough? Are they owning the mustache? "Do they believe in Rom-Comunism?"

You would expect that, for people putting themselves up for a fun and a tiny bit humiliating competition, the prizes would be worthwhile. Not particularly in this case.

Official AFC Richmond merch, which is probably the scarf Apple gave away.

There are four prizes, consisting of a "custom soccer scarf" for each of the three finalists and "custom Beats headphones" for the first-prize winner. Presumably all branded to go with the TV show.

The total approximate retail value for the prizes in the rules is $300. It probably cost Apple and the sponsor more than that to pay someone to write the rules and to host it on a website.

It's a well-publicized competition, for a premier-league brand and a return of a major show to its streaming service, held in one of said brand's most important and iconic storefronts.

Someone could've spared a few extra bucks to give them all headphones, or even upgrade the ultimate winner with a MacBook Neo with an AFC Richmond sticker on it.

Of course, this is less the Lasso Way and more something else. Capitalism.

Last week's Sunday Reboot talked about Apple's quarterly finances and how investors and analysts act despite great results.

items.title: First hints emerge about how much extra Apple Intelligence features will cost
items.content_html:
Apple CEO Tim Cook said that there would be costs for some Apple Intelligence features, and iCloud+ tier limits on HomeKit Secure Video have popped up in the latest iOS 27 beta.

On August 10, Apple released the fifth developer beta for its fall operating system updates. However, it seems the beta has hinted that there will be some changes to the way Apple prices iCloud+ for upper-tier users.

One of the current benefits for iCloud+ is HomeKit Secure Video. The base 50GB plan includes HomeKit Secure Video support for one camera, with the 200GB package supporting 5, according to Apple's support page at the time of publication.

The upper tiers of iCloud+, with 2TB to 12TB of capacity, currently include support for an unlimited number of cameras under HomeKit Secure Video.

However, Monday's fifth developer beta for iOS 27 includes some text when checking your HomeKit Secure Camera settings. Screenshots from Apple Home Authority on X when using the 2TB plan lists the user as supporting just five cameras.

Under the existing subscription model, the 2TB account should have unlimited cameras, not five. A plausible answer here is that the limits are being applied wrong in the app, and could be corrected later.

Interesting change in iOS 27 Beta 5 for Apple Home

Apple now shows exactly how many HomeKit Secure Video cameras your iCloud+ plan supports, along with which Apple Intelligence camera features are included.

But there's something strange going on.

I'm already on the 2TB pic.twitter.com/tplFxYZzBp

— Apple Home Authority (@helloapplehome) August 10, 2026

Another screenshot from Stephen Robles shows text stating "Your iCloud+ plan includes video summaries for 15 cameras." Robles claims he is using the highest iCloud plan, which would cost $59.99 per month for 12TB of capacity.

The limitation of 15 cameras is not any of the options Apple states in the support page.

Apple has not yet indicated changes to iCloud+ are inbound, and its support pages also don't mention any upcoming alterations.

While this could be a bug of some form in the iOS 27 developer beta, it could just as easily be Apple revising what it offers its customers.

items.title: RAM supply holding up iPhone 18 Pro assembly is another bad sign
items.content_html:
Apple's new A20 Pro processor isn't being cranked out as fast as it could be because of RAM shortages, and that is reportedly slowing assembly of the iPhone 18 Pro, and the folding iPhone. That's not great.

The fact that there's a RAM crisis and supply problem isn't a new revelation. What is, however, is the fact that in Apple's and TSMC's most complex processor, that uses a new manufacturing technique, RAM supply may be gumming up the works.

The A20 Pro processor is the first chip to be manufactured using TSMC's N2 node. As part of chip packaging, the RAM for the chip from Apple's regular suppliers is integrated with TSMC's new Wafer-Level Multi-Chip Module (WLMCM) technology.

In the past, TSMC has been the reason for slower-than-expected chip delivery. That's not the case this time, it's all about the RAM.

Analyst Tim Culpan has been told that A20 Pro yields are good, and quality control isn't an issue. He also says that A20 Pro chips are sitting, unfinished, awaiting RAM supplies.

This is not a case where the iPhone can be mostly assembled, and RAM soldered in after the fact and the back or screen slapped on. More than ever before, the A20 Pro is a completely integrated system-on-a-chip. The RAM is co-packaged at the wafer level via TSMC's WLMCM process, making post-CPU packaging RAM-cramming impossible.

Without A20 Pro chips, motherboards cannot be assembled. And if motherboards can't be assembled, that's a major problem for follow-on orders after initial batch delivery.

Sitting, unassembled

Apple's regular motherboard assemblers are Foxconn and China's BYD. At both manufacturers, the report claims that about $1 billion in A20 chips sit, half-packaged, awaiting RAM.

The same sources say that initial orders for launch day will be fulfilled, and no launch delay is expected. But, like almost always, delays in delivery times start nearly immediately. They are probably going to get longer, faster, assuming that the shock of the price of the device isn't a major deterrent.

This may be another reason why Apple has been rumored, since about the start of the RAM crisis, to be putting off the iPhone 18 not-Pro until spring 2027. Spreading out assembly, and therefore RAM demand, may make more sense than trying to do it all in a supply-constrained environment.

No short-term relief

We do not have the same supply chain sources that Culpan has, but we believe this report to be accurate. The churn on sources in China for us over the years has been incredibly high, so good on him for being able to maintain that.

We do know that just about everything Apple makes, including the incredibly popular MacBook Air, is constrained. Wait times for nearly everything are lengthening if you can't find one on the shelf, and that's mostly not because of imminent upgrades.

This all comes down to RAM supplies and cost, with SSD shortages and cost increases there coming into play as well.

And, like I said in some depth on Wednesday, there is no sign that will lighten up any time soon. News came out on Thursday, that US-banned CXMT denied Apple's Hail Mary attempt to try to get less expensive RAM.

This is what it feels like buying RAM these days.

Apple could buy the chips solely for the Chinese market, to try and lighten the pressure on overall global supply. But, the feds don't even want Apple to do that.

In a letter sent at the end of July, senators expressed concern about the idea.

"The limitation that CXMT memory would, for the moment, be confined to devices sold in China cannot be expected to hold, because once a part clears qualification for Apple production, extending it worldwide is a single procurement decision away," the Senators said in the letter. "The precedent Apple would set by addressing the memory shortage this way would shape the memory market and this country's security for years after supply has returned to normal, and we urge you to weigh that carefully."

It remains to be seen how that will play out.

Multiple levers, but slow to move, and everybody is moving them

Pricing is the most fluid thing about product design. There is obviously a floor to consumer pricing, based on what a company needs to make based on the bill of materials coupled with the profit that shareholders demand.

A price ceiling depends on the consumers. Apple has always charged a premium, and commands a significant percentage of the smartphone profit, with a disproportionately low percentage of shipments, globally.

We still don't think a $300 price hike for the iPhone 18 Pro versus the iPhone 17 Pro launch price is likely. In 2026 at least.

It seems inevitable to happen during the iPhone 18 Pro's first-year lifetime in 2027 though.

I've often said that Apple has the money to wait for anything. They do, they have time to wait for a service like Apple TV+ to be a success.

They can't buy what doesn't exist. RAM suppliers are making HBM for server farms because they make significantly more money doing that than DRAM for consumer devices, and there is finite foundry capacity.

Spinning up more foundries takes time. Best-guesses for new foundries coming on line with enough production to help is three years for ones not in the US, and five or more inside the US.

The longer this wears on, the worse pricing is going to get across the board. Everything these days needs RAM. Micron said that total car memory in 2023 was about 90 GB of RAM and NAND, both under pressure.

In 2026, that has jumped to about 278GB, and that's not even including self-driving car requirements, which can hit 300GB of just RAM, and 2TB of SSD storage. This is why Elon Musk wants to build his own foundry.

If this pressure keeps up, maybe getting in early on those iPhone 18 Pro and folding iPhone orders is wise. I certainly don't regret my $399 Microcenter Mac mini purchase last year. I do regret not getting my kids MacBook Neos when they launched.

items.title: Kuo pours water on rumor of $1B Apple chip stockpile at TSMC
items.content_html:
Market rumors claim TSMC is holding onto a billion-dollar stockpile of Apple chips due to not having enough memory to complete packaging. However, a prominent analyst doubts it to be the case.

The persisting memory supply crisis has caused problems with the supply chain, in both sourcing chips for products and in paying high prices for them too. While there is certainly a crisis at hand, not every major supply chain-related claim will be completely true.

On August 10, TF Securities analyst Ming-Chi Kuo wrote about market rumors that TSMC had a stockpile of 2-nanometer chips made for Apple. Valued at $1 billion, the pile was supposedly made of processor wafers for semi-finished products.

The apparent reason was due to a DRAM supply shortage, because Apple has memory attached to the System on Chip (SoC) for its Apple Silicon chips. Since there's not enough memory available, those chips couldn't be packaged.

Kuo adds that the apparent evidence for the claim was TSMC's Q2 2026 earnings call, which mentioned "increased inventory days" due to the ramp-up of production of 2-nanometer chips.

However, Kuo disagrees with the claims, because Apple and TSMC's working relationship involves intense planning. Something that couldn't realistically cause this to happen at all.

A doubtful stockpile

In discussing the rumor, Kuo admits that his industry research shows Apple's hardware shipments have been downgraded in 2026 due to memory shortages.

The key problem with the rumor is that Apple's processor orders with TSMC are planned about three months in advance. They're also based on the amount of memory available, meaning TSMC wouldn't be put into a position where it produces massive quantities of chips without the memory to go with it.

TSMC certainly can produce and stockpile half-made products in advance. But, since the bottleneck isn't TSMC, Kuo says Apple has "little reason" to pay TSMC to make the stockpile in the first place.

Memory supply is tight, Kuo adds, but he insists that he hasn't heard of any "dramatic development" like a billion-dollar chip stockpile that's awaiting more memory to arrive. "It's hard for such dramatic developments to occur," he states.

As for the call commentary as proof, Kuo points out that it couldn't be directly attributed to an Apple chip stockpile for a few reasons. Partly because TSMC's inventory includes finished goods, raw materials, supplies, and spare parts as well as semi-completed items.

TSMC also increases its "inventory days" in tandem with production ramp-ups for new advanced processes. This is not a phenomenon that's new to TSMC at all.

Lastly, TSMC isn't just supplying 2-nanometer chips to Apple. It also supplies to other firms, including AMD and MediaTek, meaning any such stockpiling would affect multiple companies.

Ultimately, while it is true that Apple is working to get around its memory issues by doing things like checking out politically problematic supply sources, it's not billion-dollar-stockpile bad.

Evidently, rumors aren't just limited to supposed specs and colors of iPhones.

attachments.title: Kuo pours water on rumor of $1B Apple chip stockpile at TSMC

items.title: New in iOS 27 beta 5: 'Before Searching' settings, updated app icons, more
items.content_html:
Apple's fifth developer beta of iOS 27 has just arrived, and with it, redesigned icons for several key apps, and a lot more than normal than this late in the beta cycle. Here's what's new.

On Monday, three weeks after the release of iOS 27 beta 4, Apple made the fifth developer beta available for download. iOS 27 beta 1 introduced the long-overdue Siri AI, while the second beta included improvements to the Apple Home and Apple Wallet apps.

The third beta brought additional voice customization options for Siri AI, in the form of pace and expressivity sliders, albeit only for American English voices. Monday's iOS 27 developer beta, however, expands these settings to British English voices.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

Still, the new settings aren't available across all devices running iOS 27. Advanced Siri AI features require at least 12GB of RAM on iOS 27, hence the restriction, meaning the new voice sliders can only be found on an iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, or iPhone Air.

As with most beta updates, visual tweaks are also present in iOS 27 beta 5. Icons for the Preview, Remote, Safari, Settings, and Siri applications have been updated, as has the Orders icon in the Apple Wallet app.

The Siri icon now features a more prominent Liquid Glass look, while the app icon for Safari now has a dot in the center. Apple has also included new update screens when the Apple Wallet, Apple Music, App Store, and Photos apps are launched for the first time.

iOS 27 beta 5 features a new 'Before Searching' option in the Settings app.

In the Settings app itself, under the Search Settings section, Apple has added a new option labeled Before Searching. This lets users choose how many apps appear as suggestions during searches, among other things.

Additionally, the Settings app now also shows when the most recent iOS update was installed. This detail could be useful for those who rely on automatic software updates.

Apple has also tweaked the Control Center with iOS 27 beta 5. Cellular network types are no longer displayed, so you won't see "5G" or "LTE" when your phone is connected to a Wi-Fi network. However, the Control Center and Status bar do feature new cellular icon bars.

Meanwhile, when a screenshot is taken on Monday's beta, the the annotations toolbar will now shrink and hover. It's a neat visual modification, but nothing groundbreaking.

Overall, the fifth developer beta of iOS 27 is a relatively light release. Aside from the updated app icons, Siri voice settings, and Before Search settings, the beta doesn't offer anything the average user would notice.

items.title: Apple preps beta security updates for iOS 18, iOS 26, and macOS 26
items.content_html:
Apple is gearing up to release even more security updates as it tests out beta fixes for iPhone, iPad, and Mac.

It looks like we'll be getting yet another round of minor updates soon. On Tuesday, Apple pushed multiple beta builds out for its existing operating systems.

The new macOS Tahoe 26.6.2 beta update has build number 25G82 and comes just four days after its predecessor, macOS 26.6.1, went public. Apple has yet to disclose what macOS 26.6.2 fixes.

However, macOS 26.6.1 fixed an issue with Screen Sharing. Apple says that the issue was addressed with improved state management.

Also released on Monday were Release Candidates for the following iPhone and iPad builds:

  • iOS 18.7.10 (22H373)
  • iPadOS 18.7.10 (22H373)
  • iOS 26.6.1 (23G82)
  • iPadOS 26.6.1 (23G82)

If you are running the beta for any of these builds, you should be able to download them now.

AppleInsider and Apple strongly advise against users installing test operating systems or beta software onto primary or "mission-critical" hardware. That warning stands for both developer betas and public beta builds.

More updates, more often

As noted before, Apple has said that users should expect these minor security updates to continue. The company will no longer delay including updates in upcoming scheduled releases.

AppleInsider, alongside Apple, suggests that you download the update as soon as it is available as a finalized release. These kinds of updates are critical for patching vulnerabilities and keeping your devices performing optimally.

items.title: Jefferies cuts AAPL target to $263.66, downgrades to Underperform
items.content_html:
Analyst firm Jefferies has downgraded Apple stock to underperform alongside a price cut, because the firm believes Apple has cancelled its all-glass design for the still-unannounced iPhone 20.

Apple has a lot going on to be concerned about. RAM pricing will just get worse, SSD flash cells are a year away from relief, and so forth. One firm thinks that they have a bigger problem than all that.

Analyst Edison Lee of Jefferies is concerned that the iPhone 20 will not be an all-glass device.

"The all-glass iPhone has been cancelled due to low yield," Lee said. "We view this as a major setback to efforts to bring in higher-priced iPhones amid soaring memory costs."

Lee believed that this all-glass body would be migrated to the iPhone Pro and iPhone Pro Max models eventually. This would, in turn, raise their selling price and margin.

So now, the analyst is troubled that the folding iPhone will be niche at over $2000. Furthermore, he says that it is the "only key driver of higher ASP and margin."

The firm is relying on "supply chain checks." Glass supply chain checks have never been a reliable indicator of Apple's future plans for product releases. Apple's glass production is easier to secure and hide, given that most of it is inside the US.

Also, finalization of the glass does not have to happen this early. Even with a radical new all-glass enclosure, which was always only rumored for the iPhone 20 with low certainty, Apple can take until February of release year to lock down the design.

Most of the rumors for the iPhone 20 have said that the device will be more like the iPhone Air, than the all-glass enclosure that's been rumored and patented for over a decade.

Wall Street mostly disagrees with bearish Jefferies

Jefferies is bucking the trend of the rest of Wall Street. The firm is one of three that have Apple at an Underperform rating. The firm remains notably underwater on Apple stock, and has not had a price target above what Apple's actual stock price has been for years.

As CNBC notes on Monday, of the 47 firms that cover Apple, 10 have a strong buy rating, 20 have a buy, 14 have a hold and now three have that underperform. Zero have a sell rating.

The current price of the stock is $310.00 before trading opens on August 10, and was $313.33 at close on Friday. The after-hours drop was gradual over the weekend, and the last few times Jefferies had a note like this, it didn't impact the market at all.

The highest price target is $400, and the consensus average is $319.48, including Jefferies. We've asked for the note in full.

items.title: Discrimination lawsuit involving converted Jewish employee settled by Apple
items.content_html:
An Apple Genius was fired after failing to meet grooming standards, but the individual filed a lawsuit claiming religious discrimination. That lawsuit has now been settled by Apple for $150,000.

Apple is a large company with thousands of employees across retail, engineering, and corporate entities. It isn't immune from discrimination and the lawsuits that result.

According to a Law360 document read by 9to5Mac, Apple has agreed to settle a religious discrimination lawsuit. The company will pay out $150,000 and provide religious discrimination training, though there was no admission of wrongdoing in the settlement.

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission filed the original lawsuit in September 2025 after an employee was fired. Apple said the employee was fired due to a lack of meeting grooming standards, but the employee alleged it was due to their asking off for Shabbat.

The Apple Genius had worked at the company for 16 years and had a reportedly good performance record. They converted to Judaism in 2023 and began asking to take off work from sunset on Friday to Saturday night to observe the religious practice of not working during Shabbat.

The employee was denied repeatedly, then grooming complaints started coming in. After a request to get a religious holiday off, the employee was terminated.

$80,000 of the settlement acts as backpay that will be taxed while $70,000 covers damages and interest. Apple has 30 days to issue the payments to the ex-employee.

attachments.title: Discrimination lawsuit involving converted Jewish employee settled by Apple

items.title: Of course, Apple's already planning a third-gen iPhone Fold
items.content_html:
The iPhone Fold has yet to ship, but Apple's already working on a third-generation foldable it could release in 2028. It's something it's compelled to do.

Apple is expected to launch the much-rumored iPhone Fold this fall, as part of its usual September iPhone launches. But, despite not having sold a single unit for the foldable, Apple is already planning for multiple follow-ups.

According to Mark Gurman in his "Power On" newsletter for Bloomberg, Apple is not just planning its second-generation release for 2027. It's also working on a third-gen model, which could arrive as soon as 2028.

When it comes to what Apple could change for the model, Gurman proposes that it will have slightly larger displays. This would be both for the inside foldable screen and the smaller external version.

Gurman's claim follows one from June, when he said a second-generation folding iPhone was being prepared for a late 2027 launch. Few details are known about that particular variant, aside from it being released as part of the iPhone's 20th anniversary festivities.

Long-term planning

The discussion about a possible third-gen iPhone Fold when the first-gen model hasn't even been announced is par for the course for a company like Apple. It seems like Apple is being presumptuous about the iPhone Fold's success, when really it's business as usual.

A company the size of Apple equipped with a sophisticated and sprawling supply chain has no choice but to plan its products and manufacturing goals far in advance.

While the public is aware of an annual cycle for the iPhone, it's really the product of a much longer development timeline. Major overhauls can take multiple years to get going, while iterative updates can still take about 18 months.

These long lede times result in a situation where Apple can have two to three future generations of devices being worked on simultaneously.

That third-gen iPhone Fold is also far away in the future that not much will have been invested into its development. If the iPhone Fold somehow flops spectacularly badly with no hope of rescue, it's a small enough cost that Apple could consider culling it without feeling that much of a financial penalty.

Ultimately, Apple is compelled to work on generations-away revisions for its products. Even if they don't see the light of day.

items.title: Ceramic Apple Watch may return as soon as September
items.content_html:
While the design isn't changing one bit, one expensive and favorite material might return to Apple Watch after a seven-year absence.

It's been nine years since the Apple Watch Series 2 debuted the material. After a back-and-forth for a few years of just white, or white and black ceramic options, Apple dropped the material entirely in 2020.

That may change soon. Apple is reportedly working on returning ceramic to Apple Watch as soon as 2026. In Sunday's "Power On" newsletter for Bloomberg, Mark Gurman states that Apple is potting the ceramic case option's return for the end of 2026 or in 2027.

This is the first time we've heard this rumor for the 2026 Apple Watch update. The original ceramic Apple Watch Series 2 was rumored for about 18 months before the material first shipped.

There isn't much yet said about pricing in the new story. But that said, you can expect it to be very expensive.

Back in the day, when the Apple Watch Series 5 sold for $399, the ceramic edition 40mm version sold for $1299, and the 44mm fetched $1,349.

At the same time, the stainless steel with cellular model sold for $699, the titanium with cellular cost $799, and the Hermes retailed for $1,249.

On again, off again

Ceramic has been a premium option throughout the history of the Apple Watch. However, when it was sold, it didn't hang around for that long after.

It first appeared in the Apple Watch Edition Series 2, with a white ceramic case option. The Apple Watch Edition Series 3 included a Gray ceramic case option alongside the white.

However, the Edition series was missing for the Apple Watch Series 4 in 2018.

The material option was revived for the Apple Watch Edition Series 5 the following year, but it was a brief appearance. It was gone again for the Series 6, and hasn't reappeared since.

items.title: RAM shortages now affecting MacBook Air availability
items.content_html:
Apple's Mac lineup has seen dwindling supply in recent months due to more expensive and hard-to-get RAM, and now even the MacBook Air is seeing available stock dwindle.

The MacBook Air is Apple's most popular laptop by far, even if the MacBook Neo is seeking to usurp that spot. Up until recently, it has remained relatively easy to find in all configurations, but that is no longer true.

As reported in the "Power On" newsletter from Bloomberg, the MacBook Air is harder to find due to AI-induced RAM shortages. Customers ordering a MacBook Air may find long shipping times given the supply chain shortages.

These problems are set to continue for the foreseeable future. New chip fabs won't be online until 2029 at the earliest, existing production lines are shifting to server-side RAM production, and Apple's competitors are buying up what little inventory remains.

Apple isn't set to debut a new MacBook Air until the spring of 2027. It's going to be a tough period especially for the back-to-school season.

While a brand-new MacBook Air might be enticing, perhaps users could look at refurbished or used models if they need an upgrade in the short term. Otherwise, Apple is steering MacBook Air customers up market to the more expensive MacBook Pro, as there is still inventory of that product.

Apple CEO Tim Cook has called the situation a "100-year flood." It may be that Apple is going to face one of its most difficult challenges in years — a supply chain that no longer jumps at Apple's beck and call.

Even if the AI bubble were to suddenly pop or deflate more rapidly, the supply chain will take time to reconfigure itself. Regardless of what happens in the short term, expect Apple products to be more scarce at a minimum through 2027.

items.title: Apple stocking up on OLED screens to offset RAM and SSD prices
items.content_html:
Apple's supply chain is now holding more iPhone OLED panels with Apple also ordering more of them, all to offset the growing cost of buying the components.

While the general effect of the ongoing memory price surge has resulted in more expensive components for suppliers, it also has other effects on the supply chain. In the case of Apple's iPhone production lines, there have been changes in the way they work.

According to sources cited by ETNews, Apple increased the display panel inventory holding period in the second quarter, from four weeks to six weeks. This refers to the average amount of time that a component will be kept in stock before it's used in production.

To a manufacturer, extending the period it holds onto components can increase the relative cost of storing it. There's also the benefit of being able to make bigger orders for components, potentially saving money by reducing the per-component cost due to the economies of scale.

A report source explained that the raw material prices to produce components have rapidly risen, alongside intense pricing pressures of other parts. The OLED panel inventory was therefore increased by Apple to stabilize prices.

An increase in orders

At the same time as increasing how long inventory is held for, Apple has also increased the size of its orders to match.

The second quarter is Apple's off-season for production, and usually has lower stockpiles of components until a rise before the September launch. This year, it's a bit different.

Display panel orders have apparently been higher than normal in Q2, in part because of the continued demand for the iPhone 17 series. Apple's global smartphone shipments increased 13% year-over-year.

The increase in orders is viewed as an attempt by Apple to minimize any rise in component cost by simply buying more of them in the first place. The larger the order, the lower the per-item cost to Apple.

Increasing orders and storing them for longer is a compromise, but one that minimizes how much of that extra cost gets handed down to consumers.

A continuing trend

While the report is about Apple's display issues, it's not the only part of its iPhone empire that has to deal with production issues.

Memory is a big and unavoidable problem. Manufacturing capacity in 2027 for the major vendors is already allocated ahead of time, as customers fight to secure a supply for their products.

The cost of memory has even led to supply chain rumors claiming TSMC has a billion-dollar stockpile of Apple chips it can't complete, due to not having enough memory to complete packaging.

While that particular rumor is probably fake, it does show that the memory crisis goes far beyond increasing the price of one important component.

items.title: iPhone 18 Pro rumor roundup: 2nm A20 chip, C2 modem, under-display Face ID
items.content_html:
Apple's iPhone 18 Pro is right around the corner, and the rumor mill started earlier than normal. Here's what you need to know.

In 2025, Apple gave its high-end iPhone a major redesign, with the iPhone 17 Pro featuring a distinct pill-shaped camera plateau, an aluminum frame, and a bright orange color option. Inside, the A19 Pro chip bumped up the RAM to 12GB, and the phone even gained a vapor chamber cooling system.

With the iPhone 18 Pro, meanwhile, Apple is expected to deliver a more incremental upgrade, with the only noticeable change likely to be on the front of the device. Smaller Dynamic Island aside, it'll be more of the same design-wise.

However, a new chip production process for the A20 Pro is expected to deliver significant performance improvements. Apple's in-house modems might finally see use in the "Pro" iPhone, and multiple sources suggest a major camera upgrade is in the works as well.

Leakers and analysts alike have made countless claims about the iPhone 18 Pro. Here's everything that's been rumored so far.

iPhone 18 Pro release date rumors

While the rumor mill thinks the base iPhone 18 will arrive in early 2027, the iPhone 18 Pro is expected to arrive in September 2026. To be more specific, an August 2026 rumor claims Apple might announce the iPhone 18 Pro during an in-person event on Wednesday, September 9, 2026.

September 2026 is when we'll likely see the iPhone 18 Pro.

Apple's U.S. retail employees were allegedly invited to enter a lottery to help organize the event. The choice of an in-person event marks a departure from previous prerecorded product reveals, but the alleged timing is in line with a typical September iPhone event.

In February 2026, it was rumored that the iPhone 18 Pro had entered test production. Based on this alleged testing schedule, and rumors from January 2026 and March 2026, a September 2026 launch date seems almost beyond question.

There have been no rumors of a 2027 release for the iPhone 18 Pro, or any other major deviation from the usual September debut for the Pro models. The consensus among different leakers and analysts is that the iPhone 18 Pro will arrive in September 2026.

Design-wise, the iPhone 18 Pro is expected to offer only a few refinements, relative to the iPhone 17 Pro.

iPhone 18 Pro colors, design, weight rumors

In November 2025, a source with a good track record claimed the iPhone 18 Pro would have a more uniform appearance at the back, compared to the iPhone 17 Pro. Apple allegedly wanted to eliminate the two-tone effect by making changes to the processing of iPhone backplates.

Early rumors claimed Apple was testing three colors for the iPhone 18 Pro.

This updated production process is allegedly meant to greatly reduce the color difference between the glass section and metal frame. This should ultimately result in a more seamless appearance on the back of the iPhone 18 Pro.

Also in November 2025, three possible color options for the iPhone 18 Pro were detailed: a coffee color, purple, and burgundy. The leaker, also the same source behind the backplate rumor, said that only one of these colors would make it to production. They said the iPhone 18 Pro would not be offered in black, a claim which resurfaced in April 2026.

However, a February 2026 report from a generally reliable source claimed that the three colors Apple was testing were actually different variants of red. Apple allegedly chose stronger colors for the iPhone 18 Pro, partly because the cosmic orange iPhone 17 Pro was popular in China.

In April 2026, another leaker, albeit with a mixed track record, jumped on the crimson red iPhone 18 Pro bandwagon. The same month, a tech news website claimed it had received a list of all iPhone 18 Pro color options. The list consisted of the following colors: Dark Cherry, Light Blue, Dark Gray, and Silver.

Also in April 2026, leaker Ice Universe shared an image of iPhone 18 Pro camera plateau protectors in the same rumored colors. Similar images were posted in May 2026 by an anonymous account impersonating a now-inactive leaker.

The same month, leaker Sonny Dickson shared photos of iPhone 18 Pro dummy units. Again, the dummy phones point to the same four color options mentioned previously, including Dark Cherry. Sometime later, in June 2026, AI-manipulated images of third-party iPhone cases were shared as part of a sketchy iPhone 18 Pro rumor.

Overall, the rumor mill believes the iPhone 18 Pro will be available in dark red, light blue, silver, and dark gray. However, a June 2026 rumor says the iPhone 18 Pro will inherit the color-changing issue the orange iPhone 17 Pro is known for.

The four colors now said to be for the iPhone 18 Pro. Image credit: Sonny Dickson.

In terms of design, the iPhone 18 Pro will maintain the aesthetic of the preceding iPhone 17 Pro. This is per an October 2025 post from the same leaker behind the November 2025 color and backplate rumors. Reports from December 2025 and January 2026 reiterated this claim, while a February 2026 rumor said Apple wasn't changing the design because the iPhone 17 Pro was a hit.

The source behind the February 2026 claim, a Weibo leaker with a mixed track record, then added yet another detail. In July 2026, they said the camera plateau of the iPhone 18 Pro would be 2mm thicker than that of the iPhone 17 Pro. They also said Apple would continue to use aluminum for the casing of the iPhone 18 Pro.

This aligns with what analyst Jeff Pu claimed in January 2026: that the iPhone 18 Pro would feature an aluminum frame, and the same 6.3-inch display size as the current iPhone 17 Pro. In May 2026, however, one leaker suggested Apple was exploring a return to titanium for its high-end iPhone models, while another disputed this claim.

The rumor mill is not in agreement about the iPhone 18 Pro backplate design, either. While a November 2025 rumor said Apple wanted to reduce the two-tone effect, one tipster, with a relatively poor track record, claimed Apple would make the glass backplate stand out even more.

A September 2025 Weibo rumor strangely suggested that Apple would use "slightly transparent" back glass in the iPhone 18 Pro. If implemented, this would have offered a clear view of the MagSafe charging coil, but the design choice has always been an unlikely option.

Images of alleged MagSafe-equipped iPhone 18 Pro cases were shared in May 2026. Supposedly, Apple plans to revert to its earlier case design, meaning iPhone 18 Pro cases will feature a MagSafe ring rather than a solid rectangle on the back. These could very well be third-party accessories, though, so it's unclear if Apple altered the iPhone 18 Pro case and backplate designs.

As for weight, one Weibo leaker says the iPhone 18 Pro will be the heaviest iPhone ever. In November 2025, the tipster suggested the iPhone 18 Pro may be 10g heavier than the iPhone 17 Pro. This would place the iPhone 18 Pro Max weight at approximately 243g (8.57 ounces).

If this rumor is true, the iPhone 18 Pro Max might be the heaviest model ever made. The current heavyweight is the iPhone 14 Pro Max at 240g, while the iPhone 17 Pro Max weighs slightly less at 233g.

Though the iPhone 18 Pro has a chance of weighing more, it might actually offer a reduced version of an existing hardware feature. According to an August 2025 rumor, Apple has simplified the Camera Control on the iPhone 18 Pro to save on production costs.

Meanwhile, an earlier report from the same month, though from a leaker with a less-than-stellar track record, said that Apple would remove the Camera Control entirely from its 2026 iPhone lineup.

It's possible that Apple tested iPhone 18 Pro configurations with and without a Camera Control button. The company did exactly that with the iPhone 16 range, and this prototyping approach would explain the seemingly contradictory rumors.

Though we'll have to wait and see what Apple has in store for the Camera Control, multiple leakers agree that a major change is coming to the front of the iPhone 18 Pro.

iPhone 18 Pro to have punch-hole camera & under-display Face ID

If the rumor mill is to be believed, Apple has been experimenting with the idea of under-display Face ID for years. In January 2023, it was rumored that the technology would be available with the iPhone 16 Pro, echoing April 2022 and April 2021 claims made by analyst Ming-Chi Kuo.

Images supposedly showing a smaller Dynamic Island on the iPhone 18 Pro. Image Credit: Early Apple Leaks/Ice Universe

However, the expected timeline for under-display Face ID shifted in March 2023, when DSCC analyst Ross Young said that the technology would not arrive until at least 2025, due to "sensor issues." Meanwhile, a December 2023 report from a different publication said the hardware was actually delayed until 2026.

In May 2024, Ross Young corroborated the rumor of an apparent delay to 2026, reiterating the idea a year later as well. The same month, May 2025, saw the resurgence of under-display Face ID rumors for the iPhone 18 Pro, this time from a Weibo leaker, who reiterated their claims shortly thereafter.

This tipster then went on to repeat the under-display Face ID rumor in June 2025, September 2025, October 2025, and November 2025. Mere days later, however, the Weibo leaker behind the repeated under-display Face ID claims said Apple had delayed the hardware to 2027.

A month later, a completely unknown leaker challenged this alleged 2027 debut date. Tipster "Smart Pikachu" claimed in December 2025 that the iPhone 18 Pro would feature an under-display Face ID system after all.

The same month, a different publication explained it was also expecting the iPhone 18 Pro to debut with Face ID sensors under the display. Apple allegedly wants to "eliminate" Dynamic Island, which the publication calls an "unsightly black oval." Per the report, Canadian company OTI Lumionics will supply the necessary components.

In January 2026, Jeff Pu said he expects the iPhone 18 Pro to offer a smaller Dynamic Island, with Face ID still present. Pu also believes the iPhone 18 Pro will offer an 18MP front-facing camera and a 6.3-inch display. A Weibo leaker said the same thing in January 2026.

The same month, however, YouTuber Jon Prosser added confusion to the mix. He claimed that, with the iPhone 18 Pro, the Dynamic Island would move to the top left side of the screen. This was then disputed in January 2026 by a Weibo leaker with a mixed track record.

Meanwhile, also in January 2026, leaker Ice Universe shared the alleged dimensions of the Dynamic Island on the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Per the leaker, Apple plans to reduce the Dynamic Island by 35% from 20.76mm to 13.49mm on the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

In February 2026, a generally reliable source explained they also expect the iPhone 18 Pro to feature a smaller Dynamic Island. However, a source with a mixed track record claimed in March 2026 that Apple would only decrease the size of the Dynamic Island with the iPhone 19 Pro.

Even so, March 2026 is when the first images of the purported smaller Dynamic Island began popping up. Ice Universe and a relatively unknown leaker, who goes by "Easy Apple Leaks," both shared alleged photos of the iPhone 18 Pro Dynamic Island.

The latter of the two leakers would then go on to share alleged CAD images of the iPhone 18 Pro Dynamic Island in May 2026. All of the images shared so far show the Dynamic Island at the top of the screen, in the center, rather than on the left.

Also in May 2026, a Weibo leaker with a questionable track record said the iPhone 18 Pro would not get a tandem OLED display. Apple will likely continue to use 6.3-inch LTPO OLED panels with ProMotion support for the iPhone 18 Pro.

Given the number of rumors we've seen regarding under-display Face ID, and the frequency with which they appear, there's a decent chance the technology will arrive with the iPhone 18 Pro. It looks as though Apple will indeed shrink the Dynamic Island as well.

If Apple moves forward with the new design, it would increase screen real estate to nearly 98%. Still, a smaller Dynamic Island was rumored to appear with the iPhone 17 Pro in February 2025 and July 2025, but that obviously never happened.

Rumors are still rumors, after all, but the iPhone 18 Pro has a higher chance of receiving Dynamic Island and Face ID modifications. Still, Under-display Face ID is not the only camera-related change rumored for the iPhone 18 Pro.

iPhone 18 Pro could have a variable aperture camera

As with the smaller Dynamic Island, a variable-aperture camera system was expected to debut with the iPhone 17 range, per a July 2024 rumor. However, in November and December of the same year, Ming-Chi Kuo suggested the technology would, instead, debut with the iPhone 18 lineup.

The iPhone 18 Pro could debut with a variable aperture camera system.

Variable aperture system claims appeared again in an October 2025 report. It listed LG Innotek and Foxconn as the component manufacturers, with an actuator to drive the aperture movement supplied from Luxshare ICT and Sunny Optical.

A Weibo leaker corroborated the rumor the same month. They added, however, that the iPhone 18 Pro's 48MP Telephoto lens, which uses a periscope lens system, will also gain a larger aperture.

In December 2025, another report claimed the iPhone 18 Pro would gain a new aperture system, though it was referred to as a "mechanical aperture" in the text.

Relatively obscure leaker "Smart Pikachu" claimed in January 2026 that the iPhone 18 Pro would feature a variable camera system. They also said Apple was planning to introduce a DSLR-like teleconverter, increasing the focal length and zoom of the iPhone 18 Pro camera system

In February 2026, it was again rumored that the iPhone 18 Pro would gain a variable-aperture main camera, with a larger aperture for the Telephoto lens as well.

According to a supply chain report, production for the iPhone 18 Pro's variable aperture components began in April 2026. The report claimed that China's Sunny Optical and Luxshare ICT would make the actuators, with LG Innotech also being part of the camera production process.

Rumors of a variable aperture camera system continued through April 2026. The addition of a variable aperture might allow for better night-time photography, while preventing washed-out colors on daytime photos.

Variable aperture cameras have other benefits as well. There are multiple reasons why Apple might use a mechanical, variable aperture system rather than a fixed one.

Smartphone cameras typically feature a fixed aperture, which is the hole that lets light through between the lenses and the sensor. This is the case because a variable aperture would require more physical space for the mechanism and motor.

When aperture size is increased or decreased, this affects the amount of light that hits the sensor. It also impacts the exposure triangle, the principle that changes to the aperture, shutter speed, and sensitivity of the sensor can influence how a shot is taken.

A wider aperture allows for a shallower depth of field, keeping the subject in focus while blurring the background and foreground. A smaller aperture, meanwhile, facilitates a larger depth of field effect, with more elements in the picture being sharp and in focus rather than blurry.

Apple's current workaround for the fixed aperture limitation is to use multiple camera views and computational photography effects to create a blurry background, known as bokeh, for portraits. However, adjusting the aperture would result in creating a naturally focused image without any computational photography.

Overall, it's practically guaranteed that the iPhone 18 Pro will feature a variable camera aperture system, unless you take into consideration earlier rumors related to the iPhone 17 Pro, which doesn't feature the hardware.

As for other camera components, a July 2024 rumor suggested that Samsung would provide image sensors, instead of the usual supplier, Sony. January 2025 saw the resurgence of this claim, though from a different leaker who added more detail.

Samsung allegedly wanted to make a stacked image sensor consisting of three layers: a photodiode, a transfer layer, and a logic layer.

In essence, the sensor would come with a processor directly mounted to it. This would reduce the time necessary to get image data to the processor, ultimately improving the camera's responsiveness in the process.

In August 2025, Apple announced it aimed to spend $100 billion on manufacturing facilities within its U.S. supply chain. Among the beneficiaries was Samsung.

A report in December 2025 then said Samsung was gearing up to install manufacturing equipment at its Taylor, Texas, factory. This is allegedly where the CMOS image sensors (CIS) used in the iPhone 18 range will be made.

However, there's evidence that Apple won't exclusively use Samsung-made image sensors in the iPhone 18 Pro.

In June 2026, AppleInsider analyzed more than 630GB of internal files taken from Apple supplier Tata in a cyberattack on its factory in India. Our findings suggest that the Wide sensor, or the main rear camera of the iPhone 18 Pro, will switch from the Sony IMX-903 to the IMX-905.

It looks as though Sony will still produce image sensors for the iPhone 18 Pro, though this does not contradict the prior variable aperture system rumors.

As for the front-facing camera of the iPhone 18 Pro, a February 2026 rumor from the obscure leaker "Apple Club" says a 24MP image sensor is planned. Earlier, in January 2024, Ming-Chi Kuo similarly said the iPhone 17 range would feature a 24MP front camera.

These two rumors can be explained away by Apple's use of pixel binning for the front camera. Pixel binning involves averaging the light values of pixels based on the pixels nearby. In essence, the iPhone considers groups of pixels as a virtual "superpixel" of sorts.

Ultimately, Apple's iPhone 17 range delivers 18MP images with the front-facing camera, and this will likely continue with the iPhone 18 lineup.

Potential camera-related improvements aside, the iPhone 18 Pro will almost certainly deliver a performance boost, thanks to Apple's A20 Pro chip.

iPhone 18 Pro performance: 2nm A20 chip, WMCM chip packaging process

In September 2024, Ming-Chi Kuo said that the iPhone 18 Pro would be the only device in the iPhone 18 lineup equipped with a 2nm chip. Back in June 2022, TSMC revealed it would launch its 2nm chip process in 2025, so it makes sense for Apple to go with it for the iPhone 18 Pro.

Apple's A20 Pro chip will most likely use a new packaging process.

Kuo, however, changed his expectations for the iPhone 18 range in March 2025, suggesting that 2nm chips would be used across the iPhone 18 line. This idea aligns with an earlier July 2024 report.

One source suggested, in April 2025, that 2nm chips would lead to a price increase for the 2026 iPhones, with Apple passing the costs on to end consumers. Months later, a November 2025 rumor from a separate Weibo leaker raised similar concerns.

A January 2026 supply chain rumor said the A20 Pro may cost as much as $280 per unit, approximately 80% more than the previous generation. In July 2026, it was similarly alleged that TSMC had increased its base prices by 10%, again hinting at an iPhone price hike.

Prices were already raised across the Mac and iPad lines in June 2026, but the iPhone was left untouched, for now. Jeff Pu said in July 2026 that the iPhone 18 Pro might cost users $250 to $300 more than the iPhone 17 Pro, after previously saying in February 2026 that there would be no price increase with the model. Counterpoint Research similarly suggested a $200 price increase in July 2026.

In any case, while a price hike appears to be right around the corner, performance improvements will arrive with it, in the form of 2nm chips. The A20 Pro system-on-chip is expected to offer a performance boost of between 10% and 15%, relative to the current iPhone 17 range, according to an October 2024 report.

Per the report, the A20 Pro chip utilizes a new packaging method known as WMCM, rather than Apple's current packaging technique, InFo.

Chip packaging represents a process applied to the die of a chip, setting it up to communicate and work with other components on a circuit board.

With the A19 Pro chips, the InFo process gives Apple a way of integrating components within a chip package. Essentially, elements like memory can be added to the chip package directly, rather than being an externally accessed component.

This lets Apple make the overall chip package quite small. Still, it is a technique that's used with a single die. New CPU and GPU combinations require new dies with this method, which could become expensive for Apple.

WMCM, short for Wafer-level Multi-Chip Module, is a different packaging technique that works well with multiple dies. It can fit together separate dies, such as a CPU and GPU, while still keeping the overall package extremely small.

Switching to WMCM would give Apple more freedom to create multiple packaging designs by incorporating different dies, and it wouldn't massively raise the cost of making the dies themselves. Using WMCM wouldn't have a massive impact on performance, but it would reduce reliance on chip binning for different product tiers.

Apple's alleged plans to use WMCM have been mentioned by multiple sources, and our own findings also suggest next-generation iPhone chips will use this packaging process.

Jeff Pu revealed in June 2025 that he also believes the iPhone 18 range will use a 2nm chip with the WMCM process. He reiterated these claims in January 2026. According to Pu, the process the A20 Pro will use is referred to as N2 and is a first-generation process.

Silicon chip wafers. Image Credit: TSMC

The smaller die has the potential to make the A20 Pro chip approximately 15% faster than the A19 Pro. It might also be more efficient, with a 30% reduction in power consumption. Apple's use of the WMCM packaging process was also suggested in a December 2025 report.

Additionally, an April 2025 rumor claimed that the iPhone 18 line would feature 6-channel LPDDR5X memory. This would ultimately allow for improved memory bandwidth, thereby enhancing performance. The use of LPDDR5X memory was corroborated in an October 2025 report, which added that it would be sourced from Samsung, though SK Hynix and Micron were reportedly in talks with Apple as well.

Per a similar December 2024 report, meanwhile, Apple worked with Samsung to change how RAM is packaged, also in an attempt to increase bandwidth.

Additionally, iPhone 18 Pro board schematics seen by AppleInsider in June 2026 suggest the system-on-chip will move closer to the outer edge of the dual-layer board. The storage of the device will seemingly sit deeper between the two board layers, which could impact repairability and performance.

The same month, leaker Ice Universe spotted a detail about the A20 Pro Neural Processing Unit or Neural Engine. This area of the chip is seemingly much larger than that of the A19 Pro Neural Engine, suggesting Apple will prioritize additional on-device processing for Apple Intelligence and Siri.

While every iPhone 18 Pro will feature the A20 Pro chip, Apple might take a different approach with the phone's cellular hardware.

iPhone 18 Pro modem configurations and battery rumors

In June 2026, AppleInsider exclusively revealed that Apple had developed two logic board variants for the iPhone 18 Pro. One of them features a Qualcomm modem and supports mmWave; the other is equipped with Apple's C2 modem.

The iPhone Air already uses an Apple modem, so it makes sense for the C2 to arrive with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In short, our findings suggest that iPhone 18 Pro units sold in the United States will use a Qualcomm modem, while devices sold elsewhere will use the Apple C2 modem.

Jeff Pu also claimed in January 2026 that the C2 would be used in the iPhone 18 Pro. Identifiers for the C2 modem were also discovered in July 2025, within an early build of iOS 18, while a February 2025 rumor claimed new Apple modems were in the works.

The same month, Apple's SVP of hardware technologies, Johny Srouji, referred to the C1 modem as "a platform for generations." Ultimately, it's not surprising that Apple has plans for the C2 modem.

We believe the iPhone 18 Pro will offer region-based configurations, with some users getting the C2, and Qualcomm modems being available for U.S. buyers, due to mmWave compatibility.

As for battery life, a February 2026 rumor says the iPhone 18 Pro battery capacity will only be slightly larger than that of the iPhone 17 Pro. Then in June 2026 and July 2026, it was claimed the iPhone 18 Pro battery would have a 4,288mAh battery in the United States, and a 4,056 mAh battery in China.

For reference, the U.S. version of the iPhone 17 Pro has a 4,252 mAh battery, while the model for the Chinese market has a battery capacity of 3,988 mAh. Models sold in China have a lower capacity because the physical SIM card slot takes up space in the phone, which is not the case with the eSIM-only U.S. models.

If the February 2026 numbers are correct, the iPhone 18 Pro sold in the United States will offer a battery capacity increase of only 0.85%. The China-specific physical SIM model would offer a similarly meager 1.71% improvement over the iPhone 17 Pro.

Battery enhancements aside, one thing we won't see with the iPhone 18 Pro is MagSafe replacing USB-C entirely, as TikToks in February 2026 strangely suggested. The iPhone 18 Pro will obviously continue to feature MagSafe and USB-C, as dummy units posted in April 2026 clearly indicate.

What to expect with the iPhone 18 Pro

In essence, the iPhone 18 Pro could deliver the following enhancements and changes over the preceding iPhone 17 Pro:

  • Under-display Face ID
  • Punch-hole front camera
  • Variable aperture system for rear cameras
  • 15% faster, 2nm A20 Pro chip with improved memory bandwidth
  • New red, blue, silver, and gray colors with a unified color scheme
  • A $200 to $300 price increase

Apple's iPhone 18 Pro is expected to arrive in September 2026, likely alongside the long-rumored iPhone Fold.

items.title: When will Apple have its iPhone 18 Pro release event?
items.content_html:
Apple obviously knows, and perhaps some of its retail staff have at least a clue, but for the rest of us, here's the best estimate of when the iPhone 18 Pro will be announced.

No question, it'll be in September. Apple has held its iPhone launches in October, but since 2011 the only time it has done that was during COVID.

The question is when in September we'll find out the all-important updates and, more than ever this time, the all-important prices. Not to drag this out, the smart money says Wednesday, September 9, 2026.

We've been here before

That's the most probable date that has been recently rumored. It's in the first full week of September 2026, which is also when Labor Day is.

Since 2011 when Apple moved its iPhone launches away from their original announcements in June, the unveiling has been close to Labor day three times. In 2015, 2016, and 2022, and each time Apple has made its announcements on the following Wednesday.

In the 15 years since that move to the last quarter of the year, Apple has launched iPhones on Wednesdays five times. It's launched them on Tuesdays nine times, and on Mondays just once, in 2024.

With the exception of the October launches in 2011 and 2020, every iPhone has been unveiled in the first two weeks of September. The latest date was September 14, in 2021 with the iPhone 13 range.

Then the earliest is a tie between 2016 and 2022, which were both on September 7.

Enough guessing

Despite occasional leaks, we obviously won't know for certain when the iPhone launch is until Apple announces the date. But the company has form on even those invitations, too.

It's a form that seems to be lengthening, too. Back around 2013, it was common for Apple to issue invitations to the launches one week ahead of the event.

Expect another gorgeously-designed invitation like this one from 2025, which will then be studied intently for clues - image credit: Apple

That happened several times, such as in 2015, 2016, 2018, and again in 2021. Then for the iPhone 14 event on September 7, 2022, Apple revealed the date two weeks before with an AR invite.

There was again two weeks' notice for the iPhone 15 in 2023, and the iPhone 16 in 2024.

In fact, from the iPhone 14 onwards, Apple has consistently issued invitations two weeks to the day before the event. That means it is now always during the last week of August that it reveals the date.

Two more dates to watch

So expect the 2026 invitation and event date to be announced on Wednesday, August 26. Expect the event to be on Wednesday, September 9, 2026.

Which just leaves the question of when the new iPhones will be available to pre-order. Typically that happens on the Friday immediately following the event, and that won't be changed because of the unveiling being on a Wednesday instead of a Tuesday.

It might be changed because the Friday is September 11. Apple has avoided doing anything on that date since the World Trade Centers were destroyed on September 11, 2001.

Then Apple isn't likely to delay taking orders by very much, if at all, but it might have to push back shipping dates. Typically buyers start getting their iPhones by the Friday after pre-orders open, and that's also when retail Apple Stores get their first stocks.

For the first time since COVID, though, there are likely to be delays in production. In this case it's because of the global chip shortage, which could conceivably mean a longer than usual gap between launch and shipping.

Or it might be that Apple launches on its usual schedule, but will then take longer than normal to fulfil orders.

That's specifically been rumored for the expected iPhone Fold, but it's possible for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max too.

Then if the invitation date, event date, pre-order and shipping dates aren't enough, Apple looks like it will have one more whole set of dates to look out for. Perhaps because of the chip shortage, Apple is strongly rumored to split its iPhone launch for the first time.

If this is correct, the presumption is that Apple will launch its biggest sellers, the Pro models, first. So the regular iPhone 18 may launch in the Spring instead.

It isn't as likely to get an event, though, so at least there's just the launch, pre-order and shipping dates to wonder about then.

items.title: iPhone 20 Pro will be bigger with familiar aspect ratios, be bezel free
items.content_html:
The iPhone 20 Pro display will be the same aspect ratio as previous models, while still being slightly bigger. Combined with the glass cover, it should result in a bezel-less effect in the final version.

Apple's anniversary smartphone, the often-rumored iPhone 20 Pro is believed to have both a glass-heavy design and much larger displays than usual. While the model is still far from becoming a reality, that hasn't stopped rumors from floating about it.

In the latest claim about the milestone release, Weibo leaker Digital Chat Station posted on Wednesday about the displays used in the iPhone 20 Pro series. Codenamed V73 and V74, the models are said to be bigger, but have the same aspect ratio as earlier Pro and Pro Max models.

This apparently means that Apple is going for a new bezel-less quad-curved design for the iPhone 20 Pro.

The leaker goes on to explain that the style of the smartphone will center around the use of a 2D flat screen with a glass cover. The cover will use optical refraction and be shaped to create a visual borderless effect.

We've heard this before...

Weibo leakers are not best known for their accuracy, though Digital Chat Station has a fairly reasonable track record among the usual suspects. That said, the leak isn't really bringing much new to the table.

On August 4, the account posted about Apple prototyping two screen sizes, measuring 6.4 inches and 7 inches for the iPhone 20 Pro and Pro Max. By comparison, the iPhone 17 Pro has a 6.3-inch screen and the Pro Max is 6.9 inches in size.

At the time, they also said that the aspect ratio would be maintained, and that a "bezel-less quad curved design" would be used.

The sizes weren't new either, as Digital Chat Station also talked about them on July 21. The use of a "four-micro-curve" OLED panel was also mentioned back in April by the account.

More recently, the glass usage was raised by fellow Weibo leaker Fixed Focus Digital, resurfacing previous rumors.

Arguably the biggest thing about Digital Chat Station's post is that it goes against a claim from an analyst that Apple cancelled its all-glass design for the iPhone 20.
