items.title: Your iPhone can capture the Perseids meteor shower if you use the right tools
items.content_html:
The iPhone is a surprisingly capable meteor-hunting camera, but it's definitely not a point-and-shoot sort of situation. Here's how to take excellent photos of the Perseids, satellites, and more.

It's August, which means those in the northern hemisphere are being treated to the annual Perseids meteor shower. If you've got an iPhone, you're pretty much ready to go take some stunning astrophotography shots yourself.

Of course, it's not as simple as heading outside and pointing your iPhone at the sky, but you probably already knew that. Fortunately, we're here to help.

Don't expect perfection

While the iPhone can take incredible pictures, it's still a smartphone, not a full-featured DSLR. You're going to want to temper your expectations, especially if this is your first time using your iPhone for astrophotography.

It's going to take you some extra time, effort, and fiddling to find what works for you. And here's the kicker: there's no universal magic method for taking the best pictures.

You'll get different results based on whether you're using a Pro model or a standard iPhone. Typically, Pro-level phones, like the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max, have larger sensors than their standard counterparts.

Similarly, there's going to be differences between an older iPhone, like the iPhone 14, and a newer iPhone.

But that doesn't mean you shouldn't try. A "just okay" picture is the first step to taking great pictures, and its certainly better than no pictures at all.

Still, I'd like to remind you of the important part here: don't forget to actually look up and enjoy the meteor shower. Spending the entire night trying to get the perfect picture isn't going to mean much if you don't enjoy your time out there.

So grab your iPhone, a cooler full of your favorite drinks, and a few friends or family members, and make a night of it.

The darker the better

If you're going to make an attempt to get some good pictures, you're going to need to find a location that has the lowest level of light pollution you can find. This seems obvious, but good locations tend to fill up quickly, especially for events like this.

Fortunately, in 2026, the height of the Perseids meteor shower and the new moon coincide. August 10 through August 14 should be ideal viewing in most locations that are decently away from cities.

If possible, try to find a rural location where you have permission to park your car if you're not lucky enough to have your own suitable property.

Non-negotiable: The humble tripod

Regardless of which iPhone you have, a tripod is non-optional. Night photography relies on long exposure times, so holding your phone while snapping a shot is a sure-fire way to ensure you'll ruin it.

Fortunately, they're also ridiculously cheap, and you can get a good one for a few bucks from Amazon.

Also ensure you've got a stable place to shoot, like the hood of a car, a patio table, or a flat piece of ground. If not, you might want to pick up a portable stool or drag along a spare cooler.

And while it's not strictly necessary, it's not a bad idea to have a remote shutter button. If you've got an Apple Watch, you already have one on hand.

If not, again, they're not terribly expensive to pick up. Alternatively, sometimes you can use a Bluetooth speaker's volume controls in a pinch — just make sure you test before you travel all the way to some remote location.

Get yourself NightCap

Astrophotography requires a camera to make the most of what little light there is. On traditional digital cameras, this is done by opening the shutter for longer exposure times and increasing the ISO to higher values.

Which is why you probably thought using your iPhone's built-in Night Mode would be sufficient. Unfortunately, it's not.

This is because instead of taking one long exposure, it rapidly shoots a burst of shorter images and stacks them together to boost brightness.

Night Mode works surprisingly well for photographing the aurora borealis | Image credit: Amber Neely

While this does great to, say, capture the Milky Way out in the desert, or even the Northern Lights in a sleepy little Western Pennsylvanian town, it's not a good solution for meteors. In fact, Night Mode won't capture those lovely trails at all.

Redditor nerdcan, for example, learned this the hard way after trying to photograph the Perseids with an iPhone using Night Mode. While the picture was stunning, it wasn't quit what they were looking for.

Image credit: Reddit user nerdcan

But that doesn't mean you don't have options.

NightCap Camera is a fan-favorite app that you can snag from the App Store that is designed for this exact scenario. Even better: it's a one-time $2.99 purchase.

NightCap has a dedicated Meteor Mode which sets everything up for you. It automatically takes about 720 photos per hour with a five-second exposure time.

If you're worried about your storage, don't be. NightCap only saves photos that it thinks contain a meteor.

Image credit: NightCap Team

However, because you're going to be taking so many photos, I suggest taking a portable battery pack with you, if possible. It's better than running out of battery in the busiest part of the night, after all.

Be prepared to edit

Once you get some good shots, don't be afraid to go edit them. You can do so with any number of apps, including the built-in Photos app.

If your picture looks a little washed out, try lowering your exposure. If the image is very dark, don't start by raising your exposure; this can introduce a lot of ugly noise into your image.

Instead, head over to your Highlights and boost them as needed. Sometimes raising your shadow levels can also help recover a bit more of your foreground detail.

Another helpful trick for any photography that might be lacking in contrast is boosting Contrast. You can overdo this, so start with less than you think and increase slowly — you can always come back if you need to.

Once you've completed those steps, try setting your Black Point again. Increase it until the sky gets dark once again, which should help to bring a bit more life back into the image.

If you find that your image is still a bit lackluster, try increasing both Definition and Sharpness. Again, you can easily overdo this.

Instead of cranking it to maximum, zoom into part of your image and increase slowly. The idea is to sharpen the edges of the stars and meteors without highlighting the noise itself.

Practice makes perfect

Ultimately, like everything else in life, practice makes perfect. And there's no better way to practice than to get outside and take the pictures yourself.

If you can, try not to limit yourself to just one night of stargazing while you're learning. The Perseids continue until August 24 and peak on August 12 and 13. You've got plenty of time to experiment!

items.title: Still simple, still powerful, BBEdit is a Mac app legend
items.content_html:
You may like Pages and you may tolerate Microsoft Word, but text editor BBEdit has been rightly earning devotees on the Mac for 34 years. Here's how.

There are very few Mac apps that go back this far, and even fewer that remain both actively developed and actually beloved by its users. And there is only one with the trademark "It doesn't suck."

BBEdit is just a text editor, but rather than this meaning it is limited, it means that BBEdit is focused. It is and always has been a plain text editor, it does not also try to be a mind-mapping tool or an image editor or a chatbot.

This is going to read like an unqualified hymn of praise, although there are actually a few qualifications. But this is what BBEdit does to you. While there are other apps I write in for many different purposes, BBEdit does what it does extraordinarily well.

I don't remember when I first came across it, but it would've been before 2000 and possibly before Steve Jobs came back to Apple. Its original version was written in 1989 because of a problem with editing text on the Mac.

After it was released as BBEdit in 1992, Bare Bones Software never stopped developing it.

The problem back then was just that Apple offered an API for handling text, but it couldn't handle large files. The creators of BBEdit were working on a version of the Pascal programming language for Mac that effectively demanded longer files.

While Apple's Pascal faded away, their text editor grew into this favorite for programmers and writers.

If you've never used it, though, it's hard to convey just why BBEdit is so popular among its users. There are people who will never leave the Mac because there isn't a PC version of BBEdit, for instance.

And as you use it, you have such a clear sense that so do its developers. This is not a day job or a side project, BBEdit keeps getting better because its developers add what they want it to do themselves.

"I use BBEdit for everything I produce that involves text: code (C, C++, Objective-C), web site content (HTML, Markdown, Textile), and more," said Rich Siegel, developer of the app, in a 2011 interview. "In a very real sense, BBEdit is written using itself — my daily-use build is the same one that's being beta tested or used in the field by our customers."

If BBEdit's search feature can't find something, it isn't there.

So an app that has been available for more than three decades, two hardware architectures ago, is still being actively developed. An app that was meant to be just a "bare bones" text editor is still simple to use, yet it has so many features a keystroke away that it's hard not to gush about this app.

To be fair, there are actually reasons not to use it, there are writers for whom BBEdit is just the wrong choice. But if it suits your writing or it suits how you like to work, BBEdit can make you into a passionate fan.

"BBEdit is legendary because we keep improving it to serve the needs of our customers," Siegel said on the release of version 9. It's now on version 16, which is promoted as having "millions* of new features and refinements (*estimated)."

With marketing like that, BBEdit remains a taste of those early times with the Mac some 34 years after it was first launched. It's serious software that doesn't take itself too seriously.

What BBEdit does and how

The short version is that BBEdit is a text editor. That's not the same thing as a word processor which offers formatting options like styles or margin control, as a text editor is just for getting the words down.

There aren't countless settings you can choose in BBEdit, but there are more than you'd like to count.

As such a text editor, BBEdit is fast and responsive, and it generally doesn't get in your way. You don't have to set any settings, you can just open it and start typing.

When you have written a lot of text, maybe even over several years, you will start to appreciate a feature called grep. This is a form of regular expression, the feature takes you beyond normal search and replace.

For instance, in any word processor you could search for a date like 01/12/2026. But in BBEdit, you can search for all dates in the document, matching every one of them simultaneously.

It's a form of regular expression. As well as being powerful, though, the BBEdit version includes an on-screen guide to help you through it as simply as possible.

"Our base started as Mac software developers, scientists, system administrators, and other technical users," Rich Siegel told Apple in 2019. "The first big change was popularity among HTML authors and web back-end developers."

Web designs can write CSS files in BBEdit - image credit: Bare Bones Software

"As word spread, we were able to help folks understand that the internet was built with text that you could treat as data or you could treat it as a document," he continued. "So the next wave brought in internet architects, cryptanalysts, and scientists from unexpected disciplines."

Those unexpected disciplines, he said, included "writers and other content creators-folks who see their text not as data but as words, and who want as little as possible between them and their words."

Overall design

Beyond the simplicity of writing in BBEdit, part of this get-on-with-it design is in how it stores your documents. Unlike most apps other than Ulysses, BBEdit can in theory be a single repository for all of your writing.

So rather than opening and saving documents all the time, you can just open BBEdit, press Command-N and be writing in a new document. Everything you've written before is still there, listed in a navigation bar on the left, until you choose to close it.

You don't even have to save that previous work before you start a new one.

But then if you want to, you can. Anything you write can remain in BBEdit's list on the left of the screen, but you can also save any of it out to separate, individual .txt files.

You can keep all of your recent documents open in BBEdit. Or don't even ever save them, just write in this text editor and export the final text to wherever you need it to go.

Then it might not require you to set anything up, and it might not get in your way, but BBEdit is built to help you. So for example, if you type an opening quote mark, BBedit immediately adds a closing one right after it and leaves your cursor in the middle.

It's the same with brackets. Type an opening bracket, and you get that plus a closing one for free. That's chiefly convenient in that it means you can't ever forget to include a closing speech mark or bracket, you'd have to choose to delete them.

If you're a programmer, that can also make the difference between your code working or not. It's easy to forget to close brackets, unless you're writing in BBEdit.

But it is also a little pain when you're writing dialog. So often you're going to follow a speech with a phrase like "she said," and to do that you have to cursor over the automatically-inserted end quote mark.

You can set BBEdit to wrap words and it also supports Markdown, plus a split-screen view.

You may well have just shrugged at that, and if you did, it's because you are the true target audience for BBEdit. While any type of writer can use it, and every type of writer does, it is best for coders and programmers.

These are people whose writing tends to be in short lines rather than paragraphs. So they may never even need to notice something about BBEdit lines that will strike a novelist or a journalist immediately.

That's how, by default, BBEdit does not wrap text at the end of the screen or at some margin stop. You could write a novel on the same long single line if you wanted to.

But then you could alternatively go to Settings, Editor Defaults, and turn on Soft Wrap. Set it to wrap your text at a specific character count, at the width of your default page size for printing, or the width of the window.

There are hundreds upon hundreds of settings you can change, but none that you have to in order to start writing. You can readily believe the gag that it has "millions" of new features, but this is still not an app where you have to study the manual.

Although, actually, there is a manual. In another throwback to the early days of the Mac, there exists to this day a 456-page BBEdit manual, and it is constantly updated.

How it got here

BBEdit began as this way to address a problem on the Mac. Today you know TextEdit as the name of Apple's free text editing app, but back in the day, it was what the company called its text handling API.

If you wanted to include text in your app, from a word processor to just labels on a drawing, you could use this API and it did the job. But it wouldn't handle anything over 32K, it wouldn't handle anything long.

BBEdit was made to show that longer files could be handled on the Mac. It did the job, it was popular, and in 1992 when it first came out, BBEdit was also free.

As well as automatically adding closing brackets for any user, if you're a programmer or web designer then BBEdit will offer auto-completion suggestions - image credit: Bare Bones Software

That didn't last. Around a year later, Bare Bones Software launched version 2.5 and began selling it for $99 (around $230 in today's money). Users of the previous free ones, or owners of various programming languages such as THINK Pascal, could buy it for $49.

At the same time, Bare Bones Software released a cut-down edition called BBEdit Lite. That was free, and users of it could upgrade to the full BBEdit for $49.

They could get it on a floppy disk by mailing — not emailing, regular postal mailing — the developer on an Massachusetts address. Please enclose a check for $5.

BBEdit Lite no longer exists, and nor does its brief replacement, TextWrangler. That was released in 2003 for $49, offering what Bare Bones Software thought would be a compelling mix of BBEdit features for programmers and database administrators.

Compared to some apps, TextWrangler did well, sticking around 14 years, even if it quickly became free. It may have seemed like it spent much of that time nagging users to upgrade to BBEdit, but come 2017, there was no longer any choice.

TextWrangler was ostensibly folded back into BBEdit and users were encouraged to move to the full app.

"We promise that you will feel right at home, because BBEdit and TextWrangler are identical in every way that you're used to," said the company at the time. "They're built on the same foundation, by the same developers, with the same care; and they work the same way."

Behind the scenes, that must've been a reason to drop TextWrangler. Maintaining the same code base across two apps was surely taking up time that could be spent developing new features.

It certainly wasn't the lure of cash from upgraders that made Bare Bones Software do this. As welcome as that would doubtlessly be, the company also sweetened the deal.

If you bought or upgraded to BBEdit at that time, you could use it for free for 30 days. It's not unusual to have such a trial period, but what happens afterward is much more rare.

Bare Bones Software made it so that you could continue using the app for free, with just a limited feature set. What it left in was generous, and really it created what was effectively a new, free, BBEdit Lite in all but name.

BBEdit and Apple

If you're a long-time Mac user, you may distantly remember technologies such as OpenDoc, but you're unlikely to have used any of it. Bare Bones Software has, it even added OpenDoc support to BBEdit.

BBEdit has been a good Mac citizen from the start but sometimes you don't know what you've got until it's gone. That happened with Apple and BBEdit over the Mac App Store.

While it's never really seen a fraction of the business that the iPhone App Store has, the Mac version has been around longer than you think. It debuted in 2011 and BBEDit was right there as one of the very first products on the Mac App Store.

By 2014, though, it was gone.

The reasons given at the time were not very specific, but they centered on how the Mac App Store sandboxes apps. Any app on the store is deliberately limited to prevent it being able to control the user's Mac or other apps.

In BBEdit's case, the app was reportedly not allowed full access to the user's files and folders. It needed to be able to open and save wherever the user wanted, and at the time, Apple put limits on this.

There was also, though, an issue of money. While BBEdit was a one-time purchase, Bare Bones Software has always issued paid upgrades at intervals.

The Mac App Store did not allow for paid upgrades once a user had bought the app. So the company could have gained a true believer but never know it, never profit from it, and that user would never know what new features were available.

By 2019, enough developers had complained about sandboxing that Apple made some changes. They were sufficient to mean that BBEdit came back on the Mac App Store, but perhaps chiefly because there was now a solution to the upgrade problem.

Apple welcomed BBEdit back to the Mac App Store with a trio of promotions - image credit: Apple

While Apple still does not allow paid upgrades, it both allows and encourages subscriptions. So today you can buy BBEdit 16 from the developer for a one-off $60, but you can subscribe via the Mac App Store for $5/month, or $50/year.

And if you were looking when BBEdit returned to the Mac App Store in 2019, you will have seen Apple rushing to make up for arguably ignoring it. That return saw an App Store front page profile of its main developer, Siegel, plus an article about BBEdit's search features, and another about its overall feature set.

At that time, Apple's senior vice president of worldwide marketing was Phil Schiller, who oversaw the App Store. He tweeted a welcome back to BBEdit, although that tweet is no longer available since Schiller quit Twitter/X back in 2022.

There's something missing

BBEdit sounds perfect. Unless you're a novelist or a screenwriter, or perhaps even a non-fiction author, maybe it is. And if you are any of those things, you can make BBEdit work for you if its comprehensive yet no-nonsense feature set appeals.

What you can't do is make BBEdit work on anything other than a Mac. There's no PC version, for example, although if you cared about that you wouldn't be reading this far into an AppleInsider article.

The real missing piece is the iPad.

It's been some years since Bare Bones Software has talked about why it's stayed Mac-only. So perhaps things will change, but 37 years after starting it, and 34 since it went on sale, BBEdit is a legend among macOS apps.

Enough so that it's one of the very, very few apps I would enthuse about this much. Bare Bones Software and Naomi Pearce helped out with finding images like that ancient photo of the boxed version, but they haven't read this prior to publication, and they certainly didn't pay for it.

Try it out for yourself. Once again, it may not be the right writing tool for you, but if it is, you'll become a fan.

BBEdit 16 for Mac is available for $60 direct from the developer as a one-time purchase. You can also get it from the Mac App Store on subscription for $5/month, or $50/year.

items.title: Apple continues to dominate premium smartphone market share in 2026
items.content_html:
For smartphones selling at over $600, Apple owns 65% of that market and grew 9% year over year in the first half of 2026. However, Chinese brands are making a dent in local market share.

Apple ships 23% of all smartphones sold globally and captures 49% of all profit. It's a behemoth on its own, but when accounting for smartphones in the $600 plus range, it's the clear leader in market share.

According to a report from Counterpoint Research, Apple captured 65% of the global premium smartphone market. It grew 9% year over year during the first half of 2026, though its market share is still down when compared to the 74% held in 2022.

The decline since 2022 can be attributed to the premium Chinese smartphone market growing in popularity. When a Chinese consumer is presented with an option between an iPhone and a smartphone from Huawei, Xiaomi, or Oppo, they choose the local brand.

That said, Apple still holds most of the market globally at 65% and Samsung at 19%. The other OEMs make up the remaining 16%.

Apple holds onto 65% of premium market share even as the rest of the market increases prices. Image source: Counterpoint

The premium smartphone market grew 5% overall year over year for the first half of 2026 and makes up a record 29% of the global market. The global RAM shortage driving up prices has pushed more smartphones into the premium $600 plus segment and price hikes on lower-end models are driving customers to more premium models.

The report suggests these trends are why smartphone manufacturers are leaning further into financing options. Samsung recently launched its Galaxy Card while Apple has introduced Apple Upgrade.

Trade-in prices have also gone up, as was seen with Apple earlier Thursday. Everything is meant to entice customers holding onto their more expensive devices for longer to upgrade sooner in spite of price increases.

It's going to be an interesting fall as everything seems to be creating quite the hurdle for Apple to overcome. iPhone 18 Pro sales could be limited by the RAM shortage and Apple reports that it's already selling as many iPhone 17 models as it can make.

Demand won't be the issue, but supply held back by global supply chain instability. Consumers may be feeling the impact of economic uncertainty, but that may not matter if financing options continue to be plentiful.

items.title: Chinese RAM supplier denies Apple's bid for cheaper RAM
items.content_html:
Apple has been testing memory made by China's CXMT as a lower-cost supplier as its regular suppliers hike up prices, but CXMT is demanding what Samsung gets paid for RAM.

It was an idea that would help Apple in the short term at best, and it was one that got it repeated criticism from US senators and memory firms. But with the global chip shortage only getting worse because of demands from AI firms, Apple asked Trump to allow it to buy from blacklisted CXMT for use globally.

Now according to Korean technology site Digital Daily, however, CXMT has rejected Apple's discount demands. This may not be the end of Apple buying from the firm, though, as reportedly it is specifically the iPhone maker's attempt to negotiate a price cut that has failed.

But Apple is not in the strong position that its immense buying power usually places it. Apple not only wants to pay less, but it also always demands higher quality verification.

CXMT is already supplying Chinese manufacturers such as Huawei and Xiaomi, and in volumes large enough for it not to need Apple. Those deals with Chinese firms are multi-year ones, too.

So, while CXMT is said to be willing to deal with Apple, it has quoted the iPhone maker the same prices that Samsung and SK Hynix are charging.

Those two firms have been transitioning to providing high-quality memory for AI data centers, rather than for devices such as smartphones. Consequently, CXMT is becoming a major player in China for smartphone DRAM.

Much of the multi-year orders for memory by AI firms is intended for data centers that may never be built. There's no going back from made HBM, it can't be converted into DRAM or used in iPhones, so there's no relief there.

At some point there may be a readjustment of the market. Apple will again become one of the biggest buyers then.

But that's not happening soon. The DRAM market isn't likely to see improvement until 2030, according to the RAM manufacturers themselves.

But for now, Apple does not appear to have found the solution to the chip shortage that it may have believed it had. And that's even assuming that the company gets the waiver from the feds to buy the RAM and not be penalized for it by losing federal contracts.

items.title: Apple's iPhone 18 Pro event won't be live, no matter how much you wish it to be
items.content_html:
Apple's employee lottery for the September iPhone launch doesn't mean it will be a return to a live-presented event. It'll probably be the same pre-recorded presentation with press in the room as usual.

It's barely a month away from Apple's regular fall event, which will see the launch of products like the iPhone 18 Pro, the iPhone Fold, and other long-rumored items. It is always a major event, with most of the tech world paying close attention.

However, with the prospect of a new CEO at the helm, there are also expectations of other changes. That can also include the September event itself.

The problem is, it probably won't be that different from what we've already got. Even with John Ternus saying "Good Morning" to the audience.

Tweet expectations

On Tuesday, Bloomberg posted about an internal memo within Apple, inviting retail employees to enter a lottery. This is to select workers across the country to staff Apple's usual in-person event.

The tasks they will take range from organizing lines, checking in guests, greeting attendees, offering directions, and supporting security teams, the memo stated. It also indicated that the event will take place during the first half of September.

The probable date for the event is September 9, since Labor Day is September 7, and it would give attendees a workday to travel.

All of this is completely unsurprising for an Apple Event. However, extrapolations by others online are raising expectations a little too high.

Live events always have a more natural atmosphere. Pre-recorded presentations have been a bit boring for years. We can't wait for #AppleEvent! pic.twitter.com/vCoInY6r7v

— Marcin Flov (@fl00vyee) August 5, 2026

Mark Gurman's post to X on Tuesday promoting the retail employee lottery story has its fair share of comments. Among expectations for the iPhone Fold and wondering if Apple's paying for the employees to be flown out, some are indicating that they hope it will be a live event.

"I've been waiting for the day they went back to in-person," writes one commenter. "Each year that went by I was getting worried they'd never return."

There was praise for the "natural atmosphere" of live events, as well as some mourning the slick pre-recorded announcements as if they are already gone.

While a little reminiscing doesn't hurt, the growing expectation of an in-person event with a live component isn't reasonable.

Necessity becomes habit

Apple's prerecorded announcements commenced in 2020, long after the last live-presented iPhone launch in late 2019.

The company had a very good reason not to hold its signature live presentation: COVID-19. It simply couldn't invite the world's media to an in-person meet-up and a live on-stage Apple Park presentation for health reasons.

At the time, Apple had few options, but it still had to hold a special event. A live presentation under lockdown conditions would've been possible, but the restrictions posed many production problems, let alone for a live stream on the Internet.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

Prerecording the presentation was the way to go. It allowed Apple to work around the necessary health restrictions, while still providing a slick presentation to an awaiting audience.

After the event aired, and the world saw what Apple could produce in advance, it gave Apple license to keep on doing it. Indeed, as the world tried to return to normal post-COVID, everyone tried to stay safe, and that meant Apple could continue with the prerecorded messages a while longer.

Eventually, after the world opened back up and the danger was over, Apple could've taken the opportunity to go back to live events. Except it didn't.

After a few prerecorded presentations, it became the norm for Apple. It avoided the problems of live broadcasting and presenting, like waiting for cheers and applause to die down.

There were no issues with live tech demos, as you would have a perfect on-screen example prepared ahead of time. It also meant Apple could be as TV-like and creative with graphics as it wanted to, which a stage simply couldn't match.

Sticking with it was a necessity. Now, it's beneficial.

But the employee lottery...

Regular observers of Apple's special events will have noticed a pattern over the last few years. That is, while there's a prepared presentation for people to see online, there's an off-line, on-site component as well.

For Apple events and the WWDC keynote, that manifests as an event at Apple Park. Media and guests are invited to attend to watch the presentation, as well as to hear and participate in some other on-site activities.

When it comes to a product-based event, that means setting up multiple areas at Apple Park for attendees to try out the just-announced items. Your favorite tech YouTubers have frequently aired travelogs about their visit to Apple Park, so it is a well-known process.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

Since there's a mass of people suddenly appearing at Apple Park, which is usually occupied by employees who don't usually talk face-to-face with outsiders on Apple matters, help is needed. For Apple, the obvious move is to tap into its army of customer-facing workers who are already well-versed in answering questions.

A lottery to win a trip to the headquarters is also a training and employee loyalty-building opportunity as well.

Apple has held these lotteries for a few years now, and they have all helped staff the in-person component of events at Apple Park. Just not one that Apple chooses to broadcast to the public.

"It's the hope that kills you"

The talk about live events can be seen as being hopeful that Apple will return to that format down the road. It's entirely possible for that to happen, but not a certainty.

Apple has found that it can create the ideal presentation for its needs. Polished like the company's brand image, information-dense, and highly entertaining as well.

It has no incentive to divert away from this strategy at all. And on a pre-record, there's no chance of something critical failing.

There's no need for smoke and mirrors, like Steve Jobs miraculously pulled off with the original iPhone.

John Ternus will be CEO in time for Apple's fall events. Expect a lot of screen time from him - Image Credit: Apple

If John Ternus is inclined to return to live presentations once again, it would require a lot of changes from Apple's production pipeline. Not least the prospect of Apple executives walking on stage and willing for everything to go smoothly.

Ternus could make that call. But, since it's the very start of his tenure, the last thing he needs is for his first event to be live and error-prone.

A few events down the road, he may be confident enough to go live. But days after taking the CEO seat, it would be an insane move.

items.title: Apple sweetens its trade-in deals, but you can still do better

Apple has significantly increased how much it pays you to trade in most devices, but you should compare carrier offerings, other trade-in vendors, and private sale values to get the most for your hardware.

There's no question but that Apple is looking down the barrel of weaker than usual sales for the forthcoming iPhone 18 Pro. No matter how good that smartphone is, it comes at a time when the global chip shortage has forced prices up.

Apple's plans to beat those component cost increases have not gone well, but it is doing better fighting the battle on other fronts. First it launched the leasing program Apple Upgrade so that up-front device costs are lower, and now it's stepped up its trade-in game.

Not everything has seen an increase. Including those unchanged ones, the range of increases is:

  • iPhone: $0 for iPhone X to $70 for the iPhone 16 Pro
  • Mac: $0 for iMac Pro to $260 for the Mac Studio
  • Apple Watch: $0 for most models to $15 for the Apple Watch Series 10
  • iPad: $25 for the base iPad to $30 for either iPad Air or iPad Pro

Of the 32 models of iPhone that Apple lists trade-in values for, 5 are unchanged, and 5 are up by $5. The most marked increases are $70 more for the iPhone 16 Pro, and $40 more for the iPhone 15 Pro Max.

With Macs, only the iMac Pro is unchanged and it remains at $315. The most significant increase is $260 for the Mac Studio, which the MacBook Pro is up by $165.

In comparison, all four iPads that Apple lists for trade-in values are up. The base iPad has the lowest value at $260, up from $235, and the iPad mini has the greatest increase, going up $35 to $300.

There is also an increase in the trade-in values of just under half of the nine Apple Watch models Apple lists. Of those, the Apple Watch Series 10 has the greatest increase, going up $15 to $165, while the three models including the Apple Watch Series 9 go up by $5.

You can do better — and worse

Importantly, though, these figures are from Apple's overall guide (and the Wayback Machine's record of how they were before). Apple shows these all as "up to" figures, and the real sum depends on the configuration of the device, plus its age and condition.

You will only get an estimate of the real trade-in value after you have gone through the online process. The actual final value will only be confirmed after you've sent the device in and it's examined.

Unsurprisingly, Apple's final price for your trade-in may of course well be lower than its published "up to" prices. But curiously, AppleInsider staffers have just occasionally found that they were offered more.

items.title: Apple Upgrade plan to preload your data nixed over privacy optics
items.content_html:
Apple reportedly evaluated giving Apple Upgrade buyers with iPhones that came with all their previous iPhone's data preloaded, but that didn't make the final cut.

Apple Upgrade is a lease in the US rather than a loan and so it's different to the iPhone Upgrade Program it replaces, but it could have been more different still. According to Bloomberg, Apple at least considered preloading a user's data.

It's been described as a "white-glove component" of the program. That means it was to mark out Apple Upgrade as a premier service, just as you could once have had the 20th Anniversary Mac delivered and set up for you.

In this case, it reportedly applied to users as they reached their second and subsequent years of Apple Upgrade. If they upgraded their iPhone, it would have come completely set up and ready to use.

That means no setting up for the user and no transferring of data, because it was all already done by Apple. It's simpler to move between Apple devices than it is, say, Windows ones, but it's still a chore and sometimes a pain.

So this would have eliminated the entire thing and genuinely made getting a new iPhone simple. But it would also have meant Apple shipping you an iPhone that had all of your data on it, despite the company hammering on the point that your data is yours and yours alone.

From a privacy perspective, the program would be advertising that Apple has all of your data. The optics on it aren't great. Maybe it only uses it to set up your iPhone, or maybe it doesn't.

The report suggests that turning on Advanced Data Protection would prevent Apple being able to do this. Advanced Data Protection is an option for iPhone users, except in the UK.

So while the report specifies that it was solely how this process could be seen as a breach of privacy, there is more. Since some users will have switched on Advanced Data Protection and others wouldn't, Apple Upgrade would have to offer different levels of service to each of them.

Consequently this does appear to be a feature that would not have any technical reason to stop it happening. But it would have sufficient technical reasons to make it a more complex feature to implement and describe.

items.title: Meta's Muse Code is yet another AI coding agent on macOS
items.content_html:
A one-line command in your macOS terminal can get you access to Meta's Muse Code, which aims to be a transparent AI coding tool that can work across large repositories.

There are already coding agents like Claude Code and ChatGPT Codex available for macOS, but Meta wants to enter the ring with its latest AI toolset. Unlike the others, it doesn't have an app interface and runs through the Terminal.

According to an announcement post from Meta, Muse Code can take on complex software engineering tasks across large repositories. It is capable of planning changes, writing code, and validating the results while coordinating multiple persistent subagents.

As always with these AI announcements, remember that the language being used attempts to anthropomorphize the tools to be more human-like. Nothing about an AI behaves like a human — they don't think, reason, organize, sympathize, or understand.

AI is a tool, and if Muse Code sounds like it could help you develop software, it might be a particularly useful tool. Developers have shared just how useful having a coding agent available can be, especially for troubleshooting bugs.

To install Muse Code, you'll just need to paste in a single command into Terminal:

curl -fsSL https://dev.meta.ai/install.sh | bash

Of course, this isn't free. Those that install Muse Code will start on Meta's contributor tier. Developers join with a pay-as-you-go option which charges $1.25 per million tokens in input and $4.25 per million tokens of output.

The Muse Code announcement was paired with the release of Muse Spark 1.2, which was trained with coding assistance in mind. Meta says the training included rejection-sampled harness trajectories and recipe optimizations for goals, compaction, and subagents.

Choose your AI partner

Meta's inevitable introduction of a coding agent was a long time coming. The company has been poaching Apple employees in its expensive chase for so-called superintelligence.

Muse Code is also another revenue stream to cover the incredible costs of AI and research around it. Meta previously tied some of its premium subscriptions to AI tool use as well.

There are several AI coding tools to choose from, so it will be interesting to observe if Meta can make a dent in the market. Not having a direct UI and interfacing via Terminal could be a problem for some.

Then there's the privacy aspect. Meta is known for its horrific history of scraping every piece of data it can from users, and while it might have safeguards in place for its AI tools, it seems unwise to trust Meta software installed with access to so much information.

items.title: New ChatGPT version has a 'Think' button, will find 'more reliable facts'
items.content_html:
OpenAI continues to churn out upgrades to its various GPT models, the latest GPT-5.6 promises to be more succinct and provide confident wrong answers less often. Here's what's new.

Apple and OpenAI have a relationship where ChatGPT is an extension for the previous version of Siri, though that could come to an end soon. The latest updates don't affect users of that specific function, but the Mac utilities and iOS app will gain new features and performance.

Now, we're going to have to sift through OpenAI's anthropomorphized language of its chatbot models to understand exactly what's being introduced here. The press release says a lot about "thinking" versus instant answers, but always remember: artificial intelligence can't think, reason, understand, or sympathize.

GPT-5.6 Sol appears to be a release hoping to address several concerns brought up by users of ChatGPT. They often complain it uses too many filler words, takes too long to get to the point, and provides affirming answers even when the user is wrong.

ChatGPT caveman

According to the release, GPT-5.6 Sol provides "more focused answers, adapts its level of detail to the question, avoids unnecessary formatting, and offers a helpful correction when simply agreeing wouldn't be useful." These problems have become so well known and bothersome users have turned to skills like "caveman" to force ChatGPT to be brief and direct.

SiriAI gets to the point, while OpenAI does shows some restraint

The example provided by OpenAI looks incredibly similar to what a user might see when using Siri AI. A brief summary of a weather result with a weather widget is shown instead of a wall of text padded with filler.

Incredibly, the release mentions "more reliable facts." Hallucinations are a part of AI no matter how many guardrails are introduced, so it'll be interesting to see if OpenAI has actually accomplished this in a meaningful way.

For example, Siri AI tends to avoid hallucinations by not summarizing content when possible. When you ask a question, the source is quoted and linked directly, which ensures random incorrect information isn't inserted. Of course, that's only if the answer is correct in the first place.

While AI tools can be used for research, AppleInsider strongly urges users to avoid any AI-generated content from appearing in a finished work. Lawyers, doctors, and financial advisors have encountered horrific problems when relying too heavily on AI to perform their work.

No amount of promises and fixes from OpenAI will create a foolproof AI tool.

A "Think" button

If you've used Siri AI, you might notice that the same question can sometimes produce very different results in terms of detail. That's because on-device models are much smaller and seek an end result that is much less computationally expensive versus server-side models.

Apple and ChatGPT have similar ideas on how to approach AI chatbots

Apply that same idea to ChatGPT "Thinking" and Instant modes, and you'll understand what's happening. Previously, these two models would be so different that the answers would vary wildly in tone or style.

The names say what they do: Thinking takes longer with a heavier model while Instant is fast with a smaller model. There's also a new "thought" slider.

This terrible naming convention is yet another attempt to humanize the chatbots, but basically, think of it as a compute slider. Lower means less compute, faster results, while higher means more compute, longer, more detailed results.

Obviously, OpenAI hopes users will change the slider for more simple queries that don't need a lot of information resources. It's computationally less expensive, uses less tokens on input, and likely means less tokens on output.

That's likely going to be useful for private ChatGPT use, but corporate users never bother. Research shows that OpenAI's most expensive ChatGPT users are in an office, choosing the most complex GPT version available, and doing so to convert a PDF into a slideshow.

It's wasteful and expensive, especially for OpenAI, which is likely giving that compute time away at a bargain. Sliders would be helpful for the company that can't turn a profit, but not if users just ignore them.

Free GPT

Free users are also getting an upgrade as everyone will default to GPT-5.6 Luna and gain a "Think" button for questions users believe are harder.

AI is a tool that is now easily found on your iPhone, which is a problem for OpenAI

Analyzing such an update can provide interesting insight into OpenAI. It's priorities as a company providing AI to the masses while developing a HomePod that can wiggle is interesting. Especially given the Apple lawsuit.

One of the biggest reasons why OpenAI has such a large valuation is because it released a powerful technology and essentially gave it away for free. Like Spotify, the free use of this technology is draining the company and all that keeps them afloat are whales and investors.

The AI bubble is teetering on collapse, or is at least deflating, even as consumers tire of AI as a concept. It isn't clear if OpenAI will find its footing before it runs out of cash sometime in 2028, or if everything comes crashing down around it.

As an Apple fan, the whole thing is a train wreck observed in real time. Sure, it took two years for Apple to find the right path forward with AI and execute that plan, but it spent pennies on that compared to its competitors.

  • iPadOS 27 beta 5 is 24A5408d, replacing 24A5390f
  • macOS 27 beta 5 is 26A5406e, replacing 26A5388g
  • tvOS 27 beta 5 is 24J5346a, replacing 24J5325d
  • watchOS 27 beta 5 is 24R5347a, replacing 24R5325h
  • visionOS 27 beta 5 is 24M5348b, replacing 24M5326g

The first round of changes included updates to Liquid Glass, the long-awaited overhaul of Siri, child-protective features, and many other smaller changes.

The second iOS 27 developer beta included an update to Apple TV in the Home app, showing it like a connected HomePod or HomePod mini. The Apple Wallet also added a new insights option, albeit in a non-functional fashion.

The third included some visual tweaks, with more customization options added for Siri AI on newer iPhone models.

At your own risk

While AppleInsider regularly warns readers that people trying out beta software should do so on secondary, spare hardware instead of their mission-critical or daily driver devices, it's something that actually matters more this time around.

It's because Apple's early developer betas are for an operating system that is still under active development. There's a higher chance of buggy, broken, and potentially harmful elements being distributed.

The initial builds are also intended to help developers learn about the operating system changes before the final public release later in 2026. It's not meant to be used by consumers.

Unless you have a vested interest in using them, such as app development, don't install the early developer betas.

Instead, members of the public should seek out the public betas. They are much safer alternatives if you want to try out iOS 27 now.

Even so, while the public betas reduce risk to your data compared to the developer betas, there is still some risk.

Find any changes in the new builds? Reach out to us on X at @AppleInsider or @Andrew_OSU, or send Andrew an email at andrew@AppleInsider.com.

items.title: OpenAI's new hardware leaks: Over $300, same size as an Alexa Dot
items.content_html:
Details have leaked about OpenAI's new hardware, and by all accounts, it's going to be shaped and sized a lot like a second-generation Alexa Dot, be battery-powered, and retail for between $300 and $400.

The rumor mill has been loaded with rumors about OpenAI's hardware. A new accounting of the device says it will be a smart speaker without a display.

Furthermore, it is rumored to be about the same size as a hockey puck, like the second-generation Echo Dot pictured above, and donut-shaped. It is also said to include parts that will move on their own, to assist with responding to a user. Somehow.

According to a report by Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, OpenAI expects users to use the device as an AI assistant during the day, similar to ChatGPT voice on the iPhone. It is expected to have more advanced models, but what that means isn't clear.

Like the Echo family of products, it is expected to learn about the user over time.

Like the HomePod, and as expected for a voice AI assistant, the device will have speaker grills and microphones for conversation. Most importantly, perhaps, and setting it apart from the HomePod, it will be battery-powered, and maybe able to be used hand-held.

But it is expected to have a camera to feed visual information into ChatGPT, or whatever OpenAI calls the model on the device.

Thursday's report cites sources familiar with the matter in saying that the device will refute allegations of abuse of Apple's trade secrets. It's not entirely clear how, given that the same sources say the device will have upscale materials and high-quality metal.

OpenAI is said to have investigated Apple's IP use in this product with an internal probe following the lawsuit. It's only been four weeks since that suit was filed, on a Friday. That assessment timeline feels very quick for a complete technology stack assessment of a product which is apparently close to shipping.

Similar assessments over Samsung's smartphone design in that omnibus trial with Apple took months to complete.

And, presumably, that high-quality metal has to be finished. A highlight of the first filed legal document by Apple launching the suit is allegations of theft of a metal finishing technique. A different donut-like shape certainly doesn't preclude the possibility of IP theft.

The device in question is said to have been designed in collaboration with LoveFrom. Notably, Jony Ive, founder of LoveFrom, has not been named in the OpenAI IP theft suit.

And the device is supposed to launch a new line of devices. Release dates aren't clear for this product, nor any other hardware shipping from the company.

items.title: iOS 27 celebrates your friends' birthdays with fireworks
items.content_html:
New in iOS 27 is a birthday reminder that means if you are on a call with someone, your iPhone will tell you if it's their special day with fireworks! The gift is still on you, though.

There may not be a smaller addition to iOS 27, but the Phone app's birthday reminder is a really nice touch. In the current betas, if you call someone, the Phone app checks the contact card you've got for them.

It does exactly the same if they call you, and it always has, as that's how it displays their name and probably a contact photo. But now it does one more thing.

If that contact card has their birthday, and if that's today, you'll get an unmissable notification about it whether you're calling them or they're calling you. Either way, unless you're really fast at putting the phone to your ear, you will see a birthday banner right there on your iPhone screen.

It's even animated, so that as the banner shows you that today is their birthday, it also has animated fireworks. You can't miss the banner and you can't miss the fireworks.

But that animation of fireworks can mean that you miss a detail. Apple's constant emphasis on privacy means that it won't even tell you a birthday without making sure you know how it knows.

Specifically, in the banner itself there will be a tiny note saying "Birthday - Found in Contacts." If you tap on that banner, you are taken through to the full Contacts card where, presumably, you can verify that the date is right.

Sweating the details

You can't really call this Apple Intelligence when it's just looking up the contact card of whoever you're talking to. But it is an example of the same thinking that makes Apple Intelligence useful.

That's because this is another case of Apple using the information you have on your device, and surfacing it to you when you need it. No passing your data to third-party firms, just making what you already have be more useful.

True, you could argue that you actually need a birthday reminder a little ahead of the day, in order to buy that gift. And if they're sitting there waiting for you to phone them on their birthday, you won't get this alert and now you're dead to them.

But still, it's a thoughtful addition and just another example of Apple thinking about people's use of iPhones rather than of the technological possibilities.

Thank you to AppleInsider reader Brae for reminding us about this!

items.title: Apple issues another round of macOS security updates as patch frequency increases
items.content_html:
Apple has rolled out another round of security updates for macOS Tahoe, macOS Sequoia, and macOS Sonoma.

Thursday's update is the second round of macOS updates to be released in less than two weeks. According to Apple, the patch solves an issue with Screen Sharing. The patch note reads, "An attacker on the network may be able to authenticate to Screen Sharing without valid credentials."

Apple says that the issue was addressed with improved state management.

The release builds are as follows:

  • macOS Tahoe 26.6.1, build number 25G76
  • macOS Sequoia 15.7.9, build number 24G830
  • macOS Sonoma 14.8.9, 23J631

How to update your Mac

  1. On your Mac, click the Apple Menu
  2. Click System Settings
  3. Click Software Update
  4. If available, click Update Now or schedule an update with Update Tonight

AppleInsider, alongside Apple, suggests that you download the update as soon as is convenient. These kinds of updates are critical for patching vulnerabilities and keeping your devices performing optimally.

This may be the new normal

If you believe Apple is releasing security updates more frequently than it has in the past, you are correct. Apple has gone on record saying that they will no longer wait to include updates in upcoming scheduled releases.

The company intends to further cut the time between discovery of an exploit and the update to address it. This is the same reason we saw the iOS 26.5.2 update in late June.

items.title: iCloud Private Relay failures manifest a new class-action lawsuit against Apple
items.content_html:
Apple is now facing an inevitable class action lawsuit over a flaw in iCloud Private Relay that exposes a user's identity. It's a lawsuit from the same firm that got a $250M settlement over Siri AI's delays.

Any Apple security issue that surfaces is a potential lawsuit target, and can quickly be seized upon by law firms smelling an opportunity. Once again, that has happened to Apple in the wake of stories about iCloud Private Relay.

The Clarkson Law Firm has filed an attempted class action lawsuit against Apple, accusing the company of deceiving consumers with its marketing of iCloud+ subscriptions. Specifically, for perceived failures in iCloud Private Relay.

Readers may be aware of Clarkson Law Firm from the settlement with Apple over the delayed introduction of Siri AI. While the class-action lawsuit was settled in December 2025, it wasn't until May 2026 that the $250M settlement details were actually revealed.

Under the new lawsuit, 9to5Mac writes that the firm is going after what it calls an "outrageous betrayal of consumer trust." Apple customers paid based on a promise of privacy, the firm insists, which was broken after a few years.

The protection of iCloud Private Relay "simply didn't work," the firm continued, exposing consumers to potentially being tracked and profiled in ways Apple fought to defend against.

Apple has yet to comment about the lawsuit.

Security flaws

On August 4, a report claimed that Apple's iCloud Private Relay was susceptible to a number of leaks in WebKit. Apple requires all browsers to use WebKit on iPhone, which means all mobile browsers for iOS are affected.

DNS prefetching, WebAuthn for Passkeys, and WebTransport can all reveal data about a user, even if they're using a proxy or iCloud Private Relay.

DNS prefetching in iOS 26 meant that hostnames could be resolved through the normal DNS path rather than through a proxy, exposing some data. WebAuthn's Passkey validation file revealed IP addresses, with WebTransport also doing so when opening a direct HTTP/3 connection.

While Apple will have to address all of the issues in due course, they will be elements that the new lawsuit will be leaning on.
